comparator: AdamW / Shampoo / SOAP each independently tuned on the same 190M base model (32L, d=512, ctx 1024, batch 128 seqs = 0.13M tok, 20 tokens/param ~ 29k steps, FineWeb, linear decay).
effect: Optimal Muon warmup = 0.3% of tokens vs 20% for AdamW; base-model best loss Muon 3.178 vs Adam 3.236 at matched budget.
locator: Appendix H.1, Table 4 (tuning sweeps; 'Warmup is the fraction of tokens used for warmup')
notes: Transfer 3 not 4: the base model has EXACTLY our hidden width (512) and the same Muon+Adam hybrid split, and warmup fraction is a zero-cost knob in train.py, but their horizon is ~29k steps vs our 600-1000, and warmup fraction interacts with horizon. The direction (Muon needs near-zero warmup while Adam needs a lot) is the usable part: at 600 steps a 20%-of-run warmup would burn 120 steps. Sequential/coordinate-descent tuning, single run per grid point, no seeds reported; grid is powers of two so 3e-3 is only located to within ~2x.
statement: In a sequential hyperparameter sweep on a 190M Llama-style base model, the optimal warmup fraction for Muon (hidden layers) + Adam (embedding/readout) was 3e-3 of training tokens, versus 0.2 for pure AdamW and 5e-2 for Shampoo.

comparator: AdamW with muP + 1/D weight decay, 190M-1.4B Llama on FineWeb at 20 tokens/param.
effect: At the D=512 base model the tuned independent WD for Muon was 3.2e-4 (Adam 2e-4); scaling either LR or WD alone instead of both drops Muon's compute multiplier from 1.4x to below 1.1x at 1.4B.
locator: section 3.4 and Figure 5 (right); ablation in section 4 'Hyperparameter and Scaling Rule Ablations' and Figure 12
notes: Transfer 2: our width is fixed at 512 so the SCALING rule is inert, but the absolute tuned value at D=512 (WD ~2e-4 to 3.2e-4 with Muon LR 8e-3, much smaller than the common 0.1) is directly reusable as a starting point. Caveat: at 20 TPP / 29k steps weight decay has time to act; at 600 steps (2.5 TPP) the weight-decay term is nearly inert, so this may simply not matter at our operating point. Single runs per grid point, 0.1% noise floor quoted.
statement: Independent weight decay scaling as 1/width was near-optimal for AdamW, Muon and Shampoo under compute-optimal training, and ablating the weight-decay scaling alone (keeping muP LR scaling) cost as much performance as ablating muP.

comparator: muP vs SP vs two published Muon LR heuristics, transformers on OpenWebText, 100M tokens, vocab 96, D=128..4096.
effect: Only eta ~ sqrt(d_out/d_in) kept the optimal LR fixed from D=128 to D=4096; RMS-matching scalings shifted the optimum monotonically with width.
locator: Table 1; Appendix G 'Incorrect Alternative Scaling' and Figure 10 (left)
notes: Transfer 2: at a single fixed width this is not a scaling question, but it is still a RELATIVE per-layer statement -- layers with different aspect ratios (512x512 attn vs 512x2048 MLP) should carry LRs in ratio sqrt(d_out/d_in), and many Muon implementations instead apply the Kimi RMS factor uniformly. Demonstrated only via LR-transfer curves, not via a same-width A/B, so the within-width benefit is inferred not measured. Toy vocab (96) is a real confound for the embedding/readout conclusions.
statement: Muon's per-layer learning rate must scale as sqrt(d_out/d_in) to transfer the optimal learning rate across width; the two published alternatives (Kimi's 0.2*sqrt(max(d_in,d_out)) RMS-matching factor, and reusing Adam's 1/d_in muP rule) both fail to transfer the optimum.

comparator: muP-scaled Muon/Shampoo/SOAP at matched LR sweeps, OpenWebText and FineWeb compute-optimal.
effect: 'Slightly better performance' than muP and markedly more consistent late-training feature-update size; cost = 2 matvecs per layer per step.
locator: section 3.2 'Blocking and Spectral Normalization Mitigates Finite-Width Deviations', Figure 3 (right); section 3.4 Figure 5 (left)
notes: Transfer 2: it is cheap and implementable in train.py, and the mechanism (pin the update's spectral norm exactly instead of asymptotically) does not depend on model size. But the measured benefit is qualified only as 'slightly better' with no number, and the finite-width deviation it corrects grows with TRAINING TIME (stable rank of the update grows with min(D, t*B)) -- at 600 steps the deviation it fixes is smallest. For Muon proper the update is already near-orthogonal, so the headroom is smaller than for Shampoo/AdaMuon.
statement: Explicitly normalizing each layer's update to spectral norm sqrt(d_out/d_in) via online power iteration (two matrix-vector products per layer per step) transferred learning rates as well as or better than muP and gave slightly lower loss with reduced learning-rate sensitivity.

comparator: Hoffmann Approach-2 IsoFLOP sweeps over width at fixed FLOPs, Llama/FineWeb, muP + constant independent WD.
effect: Optimal TPP 7.4 (Muon) vs 9.6 (Adam), a 1.3x ratio matching the 1.4x compute multiplier; optimal widths 704/1024/1344 for the 190M/380M/640M compute budgets.
locator: Appendix H.5, Figure 13 and Table 5
notes: Registered as boundary because it cuts BOTH ways at our operating point. Our run is ~315M tokens on 124M params = TPP ~2.5, far below either optimum, which under their law says the model is oversized for the token budget and a NARROWER model would be compute-optimal. But that reasoning assumes FLOPs are the binding constraint; our host is input-pipeline bound with nearly free GPU capacity, so trading params for steps does not buy steps the way IsoFLOP assumes. Transfer 2: the law is fit far outside our TPP range and its practical prescription is inverted by our throughput regime.
statement: Under IsoFLOP analysis Muon's compute-optimal tokens-per-parameter was 7.4 versus 9.6 for Adam, i.e. matrix-preconditioned optimizers prefer a LARGER model at fixed compute.

comparator: GPT-2 345M with fixed-threshold global gradient clipping; LLM runs of 9,000-36,000 steps on 36B tokens.
effect: A threshold of 0.4 prevented early spikes but failed at ~10k iterations; AdaGC runs plain GlobalGC for steps < 100.
locator: section 3 'Adaptivity' and Figure 1(a); section 4.2 (T_start default 100); Algorithm 1 lines 5-10
notes: Transfer 1 and stance 'opposes' on purpose: at 600-1000 total steps, 100 of them run vanilla global clipping and the run never reaches the 10k-step regime where the paper's motivating failure occurs. Adopting AdaGC at our operating point is predicted by the paper's own motivation to be a no-op at best. Recorded so the controller does not spend a slot on it.
statement: The failure mode AdaGC is designed to fix -- fixed global clipping thresholds becoming ineffective -- was located empirically at around 10,000 optimizer steps on GPT-2 345M, and the adaptive mechanism is deliberately disabled for the first T_start=100 steps in favour of ordinary global clipping.

comparator: GPT-2 345M with global gradient clipping at the same 10x learning rate; C4-en pretraining.
effect: 0 loss spikes and 2.52% lower final loss vs GlobalGC at lr=3e-3; 1.52% lower than the best competitor (GlobalGC+ScaledEmbed).
locator: section 5.4 'Large Learning Rate Tolerance', Figure 6(a)
notes: Transfer 2: LR headroom is the one thing here that could matter in a short run, since short-horizon runs are usually LR-limited rather than spike-limited, and per-parameter clipping is a few lines in train.py. But it is measured with AdamW (not Muon, which already normalizes update scale per matrix and so likely absorbs this benefit), single seed, and the '2.52%' is a relative training-loss delta at an aggressive LR, not at the tuned LR. Internal validity 2: the paper's own locality ablation quotes numbers (2.9639 vs 2.9712) that contradict its stated direction ('global clipping ... 0.25% higher final loss'), so its small-delta reporting is not reliable.
statement: With per-parameter adaptive clipping, GPT-2 345M trained stably at a 10x larger learning rate (3e-3 vs 3e-4) and reached 2.52% lower final loss than global gradient clipping at that learning rate.

comparator: GlobalGC baseline, Llama-2 7B/13B, 9,000 steps on 36B tokens, C4-en.
effect: 7B: 2.28 vs 2.30 train loss, 2.1% val perplexity; 13B: -0.0146 loss, -1.47% val ppl.
locator: section 5.2 and Figure 3(a),(b); Table 1
notes: Transfer 1: the payoff is small even where the mechanism fully engages, and it is bought by removing spikes we do not have at 600 steps. Single run per arm, no seeds, so a 0.02-nat delta at 7B is not separable from run-to-run variation. Recorded as opposing evidence to keep clipping-mechanism proposals off the queue.
statement: Even at 7B/13B where AdaGC eliminates loss spikes entirely, the resulting loss improvement over global clipping was 0.02 nats of training loss at 7B and 0.0146 (0.65%) at 13B.

comparator: Muon with full all-gather orthogonalization every step; Llama-style 960M-8B, and a 280M modded-nanoGPT grid on FineWeb with LR swept over 9 multipliers for both Adam and Muon legs.
effect: BlockMuon vs Muon val ppl: 20.29 vs 15.33 (960M), 16.28 vs 14.13 (1.2B), 13.68 vs 12.90 (8B), 24.68 vs 13.40 (8B large LR). In the 280M modded-nanoGPT grid, decreasing the block period monotonically decreased final validation loss at every TP degree.
locator: section 4.2 Results and Table 3; section 4.1 Figure 1
notes: Transfer 2: the paper's own motivation (communication) is irrelevant on one GPU, but the finding transfers as a warning -- if someone proposes cheapening Muon by orthogonalizing blocks/shards of each matrix to save FLOPs, this is direct evidence it costs loss, and the 280M grid is close to our scale and used the same modded-nanoGPT lineage as our train.py. The 8B numbers are far out of regime; the 280M grid is the load-bearing part and it reports single runs at each grid cell.
statement: Replacing full Newton-Schulz orthogonalization with per-block (shard-local) orthogonalization degraded both training and validation perplexity at every model scale tested, and required a smaller learning rate to stay stable.

comparator: AdamW (LR grid-searched separately to 0.008) vs Muon variants at LR 0.02 with AdamW-RMS matching; 160M model, d=768, 12L, batch 1024x1024, WSD no-warmup 20% cooldown.
effect: Muon -0.26 val loss vs AdamW for -3.6% throughput; Muon/BlockMuon/MuonBP/Dion throughputs all within 51.77-45.64 TFLOP/s/GPU.
locator: section 4.1, Table 2
notes: Transfer 3: 160M is near our 124M, single-node, and the number answers a concrete throughput question -- Muon's orthogonalization overhead is a few percent of step time at our scale, so optimizer-side FLOP savings (Gram-NS, blocking, fractional updates) have at most a few percent of step time to recover. Their throughput was measured under TP=2/FSDP=4 which inflates communication relative to our single-GPU case, so 3.6% is an upper bound. Single run per arm.
statement: At 160M parameters on a single node, Muon cost about 3.6% throughput relative to AdamW (50.90 vs 52.80 TFLOP/s/GPU) while reaching validation loss 3.36 vs AdamW's 3.62.

comparator: Adam with its own (smaller) tuned LR, same Llama architecture/data/token budget as Muon.
locator: section 4.2 Results (paragraph following Table 3)
notes: Transfer 2: the trend implies the Muon advantage is LARGEST at small scale, which supports keeping Muon at 124M -- useful as a prior, not as a lever. Internal validity 2: Adam 'failed to converge at the larger learning rates' and its LR sweep was coarser than Muon's, so part of the 960M gap may be an undertuned Adam baseline; the authors do not claim otherwise. Not actionable on its own since we already use Muon.
statement: Muon's relative perplexity advantage over Adam shrank monotonically with model scale, from 31.9% at 960M to 10.9% at 8B.

comparator: Well-tuned muP baseline with 35 hand-tuned multipliers (Falcon-H1-0.5B recipe), 30GT and 240GT runs, batch-size rampup.
effect: Loss gap accumulates over 25GT of constant-LR training and partially closes during the 5GT decay; downstream average +1.21% (Adam) / +1.10% (Muon) only after 200-240GT.
locator: section 5.1, Figure 7 (right) and accompanying text ('in contrast to simply speeding up the training')
notes: Transfer 1 by the paper's own mechanism: learnable multipliers exist to escape the noise-weight-decay EQUILIBRIUM, and Figure 1 shows reaching that equilibrium takes most of a 30GT (3x Chinchilla) run. Our 600-step / 0.3GT run never approaches the equilibrium, so the pathology being corrected has not formed yet, and the benefit is explicitly stated to accrue late and to shrink during decay. Registered as opposing evidence so the controller does not read the abstract's '+1.2% downstream' as a short-horizon lever.
statement: The loss gap from learnable row/column multipliers grew slowly throughout the constant-LR stage and shrank during LR decay, which the authors interpret as an asymptotically better operating point rather than a training speedup.

comparator: Same architecture/optimizer with multiplier gradients included in the global L2 clip norm; Falcon-H1-0.5B, 30GT.
effect: With multipliers included, early-training grad norms exceeded the clip threshold of 1 while the non-multiplier gradients sat well below it, forcing an over-aggressive clip factor on ALL parameters; excluding them gave 'significantly better' long-term loss.
locator: section 4.3 'Gradient clipping', Figure 6 (left/middle/right)
notes: Transfer 2: this is a general, cheap implementation warning that applies to ANY newly added small-parameter group (gains, gates, learned scales) in a globally clipped train.py, and the damage is concentrated in EARLY training, which is the only part of training we have. No effect size given (figure only), single configuration.
statement: Including learnable multiplier gradients in the global gradient-clipping norm made learnable multipliers neutral-to-harmful; excluding them from the clip-norm computation was required to recover the benefit.

comparator: Standard configuration where the final RMSNorm weights already act as column multipliers on the projector; Falcon-H1-0.5B, 30GT.
effect: Performance degradation (no number reported); removing the column multipliers and sweeping a fixed scalar scale instead also failed to improve.
locator: section 4.4 'Learning the projector scale'
notes: Transfer 2: output-head scale is exactly the kind of cheap knob a short-run campaign reaches for (per-logit bias/scale to fit unigram statistics fast), and this is direct evidence it backfires by inducing lazy training. Internal validity 2: no numbers, no seeds, reported as a negative aside. Direction is worth trusting more than magnitude; note the lazy-training shortcut could plausibly LOOK good at 600 steps and only hurt later, so treat as a hypothesis to test rather than a settled result.
statement: Adding learnable per-row (per-logit) multipliers to the output projection degraded performance, which the authors attribute to a lazy-training shortcut that fits the marginal token distribution without updating internal features.

comparator: Standard nanoGPT GPT-2 124M (12L, 12H, d=768, vocab 50272, seq 1024) with a learned TIED embedding table; identical data, schedule and architecture otherwise; 2.5B tokens FineWeb-Edu.
effect: 3.295 vs 3.378 val loss at step 4600 (n=3), gap SNR ~13:1, 18/18 checkpoint x seed cells favour Kronecker; ~1.43x fewer optimizer steps to reach the baseline's final loss.
locator: section 6.6, Tables 7 and 8
notes: Transfer 4: this is the only paper in the batch run at our exact parameter scale, on a nanoGPT lineage, with seeds, and it does NOT require touching prepare.py -- the tokenizer is unchanged and the token-id -> byte-sequence map is a static table built once at model init. The comparator is the main risk (see b1_kronecker_untied_confound). Note the arm also frees ~35M input-side trainable params, which at fixed width is a capacity reallocation, not a pure win.
statement: Replacing the learned input embedding table with a fixed byte-position Kronecker codec feeding a single learned D->d_model projection reduced validation loss by 0.083 +/- 0.007 nats (2.5%) on GPT-2 124M trained 4,600 steps on FineWeb-Edu, over 3 seeds per arm.

comparator: Same run as b1_kronecker_byte_embed_124m_win (BPE-tied arm, per-200-step checkpoints).
locator: section 6.6 Table 7 and 'Gap behavior'
notes: This is the number that decides whether the lever is worth a slot at OUR horizon. At 600-1000 steps we should expect roughly 0.02-0.07 nats, not the headline 0.083 -- still large versus our measured 5-min-frame noise floor (sigma ~0.0006) but a factor of 2-4 smaller than advertised. Their step is 0.54M tokens (batch inferred from 2.5B/4600) which is close to our 0.524M, so the step axis is roughly comparable. Transfer 3 rather than 4 because the early-checkpoint values are read off a single 'representative run' table, not the 3-seed summary.
statement: The Kronecker-vs-BPE validation-loss gap was small early and only saturated after roughly 2,000 optimizer steps: 0.015 nats at step 200, 0.071 at step 1,000, 0.083 at step 2,000, then flat to step 4,600.

comparator: BPE embedding gather (essentially zero compute) in the same 124M nanoGPT training loop.
effect: +1.2% per-step time; net time to reach the baseline's converged loss ~= (1/1.43)*1.012 ~= 0.71 of baseline wall-clock. At production vocab (131k, D=8192) the on-the-fly variant costs only 0.01-0.24% of step time.
locator: section 6.6 'Per-step wall-clock at this scale' and section 6.9
notes: Transfer 3: the overhead is pure GPU FLOPs, which our host has spare (v3 scope is input-pipeline bound), so 1.2% is likely an over-estimate for us -- and it can be reduced to near zero by precomputing the full |V| x d_model effective embedding once per step instead of per token. Internal validity 2: reported as a single measured percentage with no distribution, on unspecified hardware.
statement: The Kronecker input pathway cost about 1.2% more wall-clock per step than a BPE gather at the 124M scale, the overhead being the single D->d_model matrix multiply.

comparator: BPE-tied only; no BPE-untied control at either 124M or 138M.
effect: Kronecker arm carries a standalone 38.6M untied lm_head, making it +3.1M total trainable params versus the tied baseline; the authors state the three-arm comparison is future work.
locator: section 6.6 'Limitations of this run'; section 8.2 'Untied-BPE baseline'; section 3.5 (tying architecturally inapplicable)
notes: Directly load-bearing for us: our train.py already uses an untied head plus value embeddings, so the portion of the 0.083-nat gap that comes from untying is already banked and would NOT be re-earned. Registered as 'opposes' because it is the reason to discount the headline effect before spending a slot. Transfer 3: the confound is concrete and the fix (run our own untied control) is cheap at 300s per run.
statement: Both Kronecker training comparisons used a weight-TIED BPE baseline and no untied-BPE arm was run, so the reported gap conflates the byte codec with the effect of untying the output head.

comparator: RMSNorm followed by MXLinear, Llama 3 on SlimPajama, LR swept 2^-14..2^-3, TorchTitan FSDP bf16.
locator: section 4.1, Figure 4 and accompanying text
notes: Transfer 2 and stance opposes: their 125M model is depth 8 like ours (width 1024 vs our 512), so this is the closest available evidence, and it says a cheaper approximate normalization costs ~0.025 loss at OUR scale even though it is free at 1B. Generalizes as a caution that norm-path approximations are scale-sensitive in the wrong direction for us. The +/- values give a useful cross-check on their measurement noise (0.004-0.012 at 125M).
statement: Approximating RMSNorm by reusing MXFP block absmaxes matched RMSNorm at 1B but was slightly WORSE at 125M, with final training loss 3.113-3.116 versus 3.090 for RMSNorm.

comparator: RMSNorm fused with MXCast, torch.compile-generated kernels on GB200.
effect: Kernel-level 41.7% (MXFP8 B=32) / 31.2% (NVFP4 B=16) -> block-level 1.3% / 2.6%.
locator: section 4.3 'Performance Analysis', Figure 9 and accompanying text
notes: Transfer 2 as a negative systems result: normalization is a ~3% share of block time even in low precision, so optimizing the norm path cannot buy meaningful steps in a 300s budget -- and our profile already says the bottleneck is the CPU-side packing loop and small n-gram GEMMs, not norms. Measured on GB200 with MX formats we do not use; the ratio (kernel win -> end-to-end win) is the transferable part, not the absolute numbers.
statement: A 31-42% speedup of the isolated normalization+cast kernel translated to only 1.3% (MXFP8) and 2.6% (NVFP4) geometric-mean speedup of the full transformer block at 8B hidden dimension 4096.

comparator: Cosine, WSD (exponential decay) and WSDLD (linear decay) with grid-searched decay ratios; Llama-2 25M/100M/400M/1B, AdamW, peak LR 3e-4, batch 0.5M tokens, 24k-72k steps.
effect: Symbolic regression on the optimized schedule gives exponent 1.5; WSDSC beats WSD at 25M-1B and on GPT-2, though still below the fully optimized schedule. Optimized schedules beat cosine by a margin exceeding 0.02 loss.
locator: section 6.2 'Optimized LR Schedule Outperforms Tuned WSD Variants'; Figures 9(b) and 13(a)
notes: Transfer 3: changing the decay function is a literally free edit to train.py and the shape claim is architecture- and size-robust in their ablations (GPT-2 and OLMo included). Discounted from 4 because every run has a 2160-step warmup and >=16k post-warmup steps; our entire run is shorter than their warmup, and MPL is fitted on decaying schedules with a converged warmup, so the optimal exponent at 600 steps is an extrapolation. Also all their runs use AdamW, not Muon.
statement: The LR-schedule shape found by minimizing the fitted Multi-Power Law is warmup-stable-decay with a power decay eta_t = eta_max*(1-tau)^1.5 rather than linear or exponential, and this sqrt-cube variant (WSDSC) outperformed standard WSD across model sizes and architectures.

comparator: WSD and WSDLD with decay ratio grid-searched over five values; 400M Llama-2, 12B tokens.
effect: Optimal decay phase ~= 6,000 / 24,000 = 25% of total steps; the optimized schedule decays to below 1/20 of peak LR (vs 1/10 for standard WSD), but setting the end LR near zero alone does NOT close the gap to the optimized schedule.
locator: section 6.2 'Optimized LR Schedule Outperforms Tuned WSD Variants' (grid over {3000,4000,5000,6000,7000})
notes: Transfer 2: the 25% cooldown fraction is a concrete starting point (=~150 steps of a 600-step run) but it was tuned at a 24k-step horizon where the stable phase has time to do its work; short runs typically want a LARGER decay fraction, so this number may be a lower bound for us. The secondary finding -- end-LR near zero is necessary but not sufficient, the decay SHAPE carries the gain -- is the more robust part.
statement: For a 400M model over 24,000 steps the MPL-optimized schedule's decay onset coincided with the grid-searched optimum for WSD, at about 6,000 steps of a 24,000-step run.

comparator: Chinchilla data-scaling law fitted on six run endpoints, and the Momentum Law; Llama-2 25M-1B plus GPT-2 and 7B OLMo curves.
effect: R^2 0.9975/0.9982/0.9971 at 25M/100M/400M vs Momentum Law 0.9904/0.9959/0.9962; final-loss prediction error under 1/3 of a Chinchilla-style fit at ~1/5 the compute; seed noise floor ~0.001 loss std at 25M/24k steps.
locator: section 5.1-5.3, Table 1; Figure 8(a)
notes: Transfer 3 as a METHOD rather than an intervention: our runs cost 300s, so fitting MPL on 2-3 of our own curves and numerically optimizing the 600-step schedule is affordable and would be fitted AT our operating point, which sidesteps the horizon-extrapolation objection to their schedule findings. Caveats they state: accuracy degrades as peak LR rises (R^2 0.9965 at 4e-4, 0.9940 at 6e-4), coefficients are batch-size dependent, the law assumes monotone decay after warmup and fresh samples every step (single-epoch, which we satisfy).
statement: The Multi-Power Law predicted full loss curves for unseen LR schedules and 3x-longer horizons after being fitted on as few as two or three training curves, with R^2 >= 0.997 and worst-case error <= 0.007 at 25M-400M.

comparator: n/a (scope statement).
effect: Warmup contributes only through the scalar S_W = 0.5*eta_max*W in the law; shortest studied post-warmup horizon is ~16,000 steps.
locator: section 1 (problem restrictions), section 2 'Warmup Phase', section 5.1 experiment setting
notes: Boundary rather than support: our entire 600-1000 step run is shorter than their warmup phase, so any MPL-derived schedule must be refitted at our horizon before it means anything. Recorded so schedule claims from this paper are not applied verbatim. Also the law neglects model-size dependence and is fitted per-configuration.
statement: Every Multi-Power Law experiment fixes a 2,160-step warmup and studies only the post-warmup schedule, explicitly assuming the warmup shape and peak LR were already tuned by separate short runs.

comparator: NorMuon at its own tuned eta=0.01, mu=0.9; dense transformers 1B-14B on ClimbMix, FSDP with MXFP8 weights, GQA + sliding-window attention.
effect: Best loss at f=1/8 for 1B/100B tokens, all f<1 variants finishing ~0.01 below fully tuned NorMuon; at 10B tokens Dion3 f=1/4 beat NorMuon at every size (-0.012 at 3B to -0.027 at 14B). Optimal LR tracks eta*sqrt(f) = 0.01.
locator: section 6 (Algorithm 4), section 8.1 'Learning-rate transfer rule' and 'Dion3 improves the loss', Figures 3-5 and Table 2
notes: Transfer 2: it is a MECHANISM (selective update + error feedback) implementable in train.py, and the eta ~ 1/sqrt(f) rule is derived from update Frobenius norm so it is size-independent. But every measurement is at >=1B params on >=10B tokens, the effect (0.01-0.027 nats) is near their own resolution with single runs per cell, and the compute motivation is absent for us: at 124M with 512-wide matrices Newton-Schulz is already a few percent of step time, so f<1 buys almost no steps. Worth testing only for the loss effect, and only if a cheaper lever is not queued.
statement: Orthogonalizing only a fraction f of the momentum matrix rows each step (with error feedback on the unselected rows) and scaling the learning rate as eta ~ 1/sqrt(f) matched or slightly beat full-matrix Muon/NorMuon in validation loss at 1B-14B parameters.

comparator: Standard Newton-Schulz with Polar Express coefficients, Muon on Hopper GPUs.
effect: (4T+3alpha-3)n^3 vs T(3alpha+1)n^3 FLOPs; 55% saving at T=5, alpha=4 with symmetric GEMMs (68% without); restart costs 3(alpha-1)n^3; naive version diverged when training Llama-430M in half precision. Kernelized Gram-NS preserved validation perplexity to within 0.01.
locator: sections 4, 4.1, 4.2 (Algorithm 3); Appendix B.1 and Figures 11-14
notes: Transfer 2: our MLP weights are 512x2048 (alpha=4) so the FLOP saving applies exactly, and a pip-installable implementation exists -- but our Newton-Schulz cost is already a small share of a step that is input-pipeline bound, so the ceiling on the win is low. The load-bearing part for us is the numerical warning: any bf16 Gram-based or squared-matrix reformulation of the orthogonalization is unstable without a restart, and that failure is silent (quality loss) not loud.
statement: Running Newton-Schulz on the Gram matrix X X^T is mathematically identical to standard Newton-Schulz and 55% cheaper in FLOPs at aspect ratio 4, but destabilizes and can diverge in half precision because rounding produces spurious negative eigenvalues; a mid-iteration restart plus float16 (not bfloat16) was required to preserve training quality.

comparator: The same Dion3 update rule with the fused single-operation weight update.
effect: Loss regression versus Muon/NorMuon attributed entirely to lost fusion; also required NorMuon's normalization step to be done in float32.
locator: section 6 'Weight Update' (paragraph on the 'nefarious numerical issue')
notes: Transfer 3: our train.py is torch.compile'd and bf16, so this is a live hazard for ANY optimizer edit we make -- a change can regress val_bpb through casting rounds rather than through the algorithm, which would be misread as the mechanism failing. Cheap to guard: check the number of casts / kernel fusions before and after any optimizer change. No effect size given, which is the only reason this is not internal_validity 4.
statement: Introducing a row-selection operator into the weight update broke the compiler's fusion of the decay-plus-update into one bf16->fp32->bf16 round trip, creating extra up/down-casts that made the optimizer underperform Muon on final loss until a custom Triton kernel restored the original numerics.

comparator: AdamW with the same cosine schedule, weight decay 0.05, 256k-token batch, LR swept on a power-of-two grid 0.001-0.02 separately for each optimizer; 120M Llama-3 on 200B tokens of FineWeb-Edu.
effect: Removes the >2x gradient-norm increase in the second half of training and stabilizes weight norms; loss described as 'notably lower' (no number given).
locator: section 5 (Algorithm 1) and section 6, Figure 4
notes: Transfer 1 despite the model being 120M -- almost exactly our size -- because the horizon is 200B tokens (~760k steps at their batch) versus our ~0.3B, and the mechanism requires the weights to have reached the weight-decay/noise steady state and then be dragged by a decaying LR. The correction is a one-line change and costs nothing, so it is cheap to test, but the theory predicts it is a no-op for us. No effect size and no seeds are reported for the LLM run (5 seeds only for the ImageNet run).
statement: Scaling weight decay on normalized layers by gamma_t/gamma_max (AdamC) removed the end-of-training gradient-norm blow-up and gave notably lower loss throughout training for a 120M Llama-3 model on FineWeb-Edu.

It also implies weight decay itself is close to inert at our horizon, which bears on b1_indep_wd_scales_inverse_width.

This is an argument about arithmetic that transfers cleanly; it is not an empirical result on our hardware, and our host is CPU/input-pipeline bound rather than GPU bound, which only strengthens the conclusion.

The favourable region is a narrow (alpha,beta) wedge whose parameters we cannot measure for FineWeb. Numbers are exponents in a toy risk, not nats.

Out of regime -- this paper should not license a schedule change on its own.

The unbounded-weight-growth failure mode that motivates WD cannot develop in 600 steps. comparator: vanilla Muon with Keller Jordan's tuned airbench hyperparameters (10 repetitions per alpha) and the NanoGPT speedrun baseline
effect: NanoGPT alpha=1.1: 3.2818 vs Muon 3.279; CIFAR airbench tuned F-Muon 94.02+/-0.13% over 200 runs vs Muon's matching accuracy and variance; S-Muon 94.03+/-0.13%
locator: section 6.2 (CIFAR airbench, 200 runs) and section 6.3 (alpha=1.1 result); section 8
notes: transfer=3: the CIFAR arm is the only properly replicated experiment in this entire batch (200 runs, explicit variance), and it says the update-geometry knob is flat. Read together with the null NanoGPT result, this is strong evidence that the norm/geometry axis of Muon is SATURATED and should be de-prioritized in favour of structural levers. Boundary rather than opposes because it is a statement about insensitivity, not about harm. CIFAR-10 image classification obviously does not transfer on its own; the NanoGPT arm carries the weight.
statement: Performance was remarkably insensitive to the shape of the LMO constraint region: even alpha=1.1, a configuration whose constraint region is not a norm ball at all, gave a NanoGPT loss of 3.2818 versus Muon's 3.279, and tuned F-Muon matched Muon's accuracy and variance on CIFAR-10 airbench.

comparator: Kimi-variant Muon at the same LR, beta=0.95, wd 0.1, on nanoGPT-style GPT-2 Small 125M, OpenWebText, ctx 1024, effective batch 60 sequences (~61k tokens/step), 100k steps, warmup-stable schedule
effect: sign-only variant below the Muon training-loss curve; full method (sign + second moment on the NS output + RMS realignment) best overall
locator: section 4.3 Ablation Study, Figure 3 (GPT-2 Small and Qwen2.5-1.5B); Theorem 1 in section 3.2
notes: transfer=3: a one-line, throughput-free change to the momentum buffer just before Newton-Schulz, and it is the same 'normalize elementwise BEFORE orthogonalizing' family that 2601.14603 and 2604.09967 independently support -- three separate papers pointing at the pre-NS position is the strongest cross-paper signal in this batch. Docked from 4 because the ablation is a figure with no numbers or seeds, the runs are 100k steps at 61k tokens/step (a low-noise-per-step regime unlike our 524k-token batch, where sign's noise-suppression rationale is weaker), and 2604.09967 Table 3 reports that full AdaMuon LOST to plain Muon on GPT-Base.
statement: In an ablation, applying the sign transform to the momentum before the polar/Newton-Schulz step ALONE already yielded lower training loss than plain Muon, and the authors prove sign is the unique elementwise map that is scale-invariant, sign-consistent, odd and bounded.

comparator: plain Muon (Kimi variant) on GPT-2 Small 125M / OpenWebText, same setup as the main runs
effect: second-momentum-only variant underperforms Muon ('Muon even outperforms this variant'); only the combination with sign recovers and surpasses Muon
locator: section 4.3 Ablation Study, Figure 3; section 2.3.2 'Challenges'
notes: transfer=3: important opposing evidence that constrains WHERE in the Muon pipeline an adaptive rescale may be inserted. Post-orthogonalization elementwise adaptivity is reported as harmful on its own here, and 2601.14603's post-ortho ablation independently found the same ordering effect (post-ortho underperforms Muon early). If we test adaptive Muon at all, put the rescale on the momentum/gradient before Newton-Schulz, not on its output. Figure-only, no numbers or seeds.
statement: Adding an elementwise second-moment normalization on the Newton-Schulz OUTPUT without the sign stabilization was worse than plain Muon; the authors attribute this to the orthogonalized update being too unstable elementwise for the accumulated variance to be meaningful.

comparator: same model/LR (6e-4), GPT-2 Small 125M, only beta varied
effect: final train loss 2.96107 (beta=0.8), 2.95735 (0.9), 2.95521 (0.95), 2.95487 (0.99) -- total spread 0.0062 nats, monotone but flat above 0.9
locator: section 4.5 Sensitivity Analysis, Table 3
notes: transfer=3: a saturated-knob finding, which this campaign should treat as a do-not-spend signal: beta is not worth an experiment slot. Measured at 100k steps though, and momentum warmup effects at step 600 are a different question -- an EMA with beta=0.95 has a ~20-step horizon and is fully warmed by then, so the flatness plausibly holds. Single runs, no seeds; the 0.006 spread is comparable to seed noise, which only reinforces 'flat'.
statement: Varying the momentum/second-moment coefficient beta over 0.8, 0.9, 0.95 and 0.99 changed the final GPT-2 Small training loss by only about 0.006, indicating low sensitivity across the standard band.

comparator: AdamW baseline at 49.2B tokens, same nanoGPT architecture (RoPE, no bias, warmup-stable schedule), 100k steps, ctx 1024, effective batch 60 sequences
effect: GPT-2 Small val: AdaMuon 33.73% vs Muon 21.57% token savings at LR 6e-4; at LR 1e-3, 38.81% vs 25.46%; consistent across four scales
locator: section 4.2 Table 1
notes: transfer=2: the metric is tokens-to-match-AdamW's FINAL loss after 100k steps, which is a long-horizon statement and says nothing about the first 600 steps; the batch (61k tokens/step) is 8.6x smaller than ours, so the gradient-noise regime that AdaMuon's variance adaptivity exploits is much noisier than ours. Directly contradicted in part by 2604.09967 Table 3, where AdaMuon underperformed plain Muon on GPT-Base at both NS settings (26.07 vs 24.69 at Ns=3; 22.42 vs 21.47 at Ns=5) -- so the headline should not be taken at face value without an independent check.
statement: AdaMuon reached AdamW's 49.2B-token validation loss using 33.7% fewer tokens on GPT-2 Small, versus 21.6% fewer for Muon, with the ordering preserved across GPT-2 Small/Medium/Large/XL and two learning rates.

comparator: 6B MoE trained from scratch under the same total FLOPs; growth is 3B->6B depth growth by layer interposition
effect: end accuracy 48.53 (grow at 16k) vs 45.03 (scratch, 0k) vs 46.12 (grow at 64k); heuristic given: allocate post-growth FLOPs at least on the same order as the sunk cost
locator: section 4.2, Figure 8 and Table 2
notes: transfer=1: the mechanism (spend early FLOPs on a smaller model, then grow, within one fixed budget) is in principle expressible inside a single 300s run and does not touch prepare.py, which is why it is not scored 0. But the evidence is 3B->6B MoE at ~10^20 FLOPs, the reported metric is average downstream benchmark accuracy rather than validation loss, and the paper explicitly notes the grown models' TRAINING LOSS stays relatively high while accuracy recovers -- which is the wrong direction for a val_bpb objective. Growth also requires an optimizer-state and LR-schedule reset whose cost at 600 steps is unbounded. Out of regime as evidence; usable only as a hypothesis generator.
statement: At a fixed TOTAL FLOPs budget, growing a model from an early checkpoint (16k of ~96k steps) reached higher final downstream accuracy than training the target-size model from scratch, while growth from late checkpoints (insufficient post-growth budget) underperformed.

comparator: stack growth (layers concatenated k times) from the same checkpoint, compared on a total-FLOPs x-axis
effect: interposition beats stack on both training loss and average downstream accuracy at 3B->6B, replicated at 17B->34B; rationale is preserving the characteristic increasing-then-slightly-decreasing layer-norm profile
locator: section 3.1, Figure 3 and Figure 2 (layer-wise weight norm profile); section 5 Figure 9 (17B replication)
notes: transfer=2: the useful content for us is the boundary condition, not the recommendation. Our entire run lives in the early regime the authors explicitly exclude -- at 600 steps layer roles have not specialized and the layer-norm profile they rely on has not formed -- so if any depth-growth idea is tried here, the prior literature's STACK variant is the indicated one, not this paper's interposition. Evidence is MoE at 3B-34B with downstream-accuracy curves; no small-scale or short-horizon check is offered.
statement: For well-converged checkpoints, duplicating each layer in place (interposition) beat concatenating the whole layer stack, while the authors note that prior work advocating stacking studied the EARLY stages of training before layer parameter distributions had diverged.

comparator: plain Muon with the original polar coefficients, best over a 5-point LR sweep for EACH method separately; GPT models on FineWeb with the GPT tokenizer at compute-optimal budgets (GPT-Small 3.0B tokens), LLaMA models on C4 (LLaMA-60M 1.0B tokens), NanoGPT/Nanotron pipelines on H100/A100
locator: section 3.1 Algorithm 1; section 4.1 Table 1 and section 4.2 Table 2; Appendix C Tables 5-11 (LR sweeps)
notes: transfer=3: the strongest-designed optimizer result in this batch -- per-method LR sweeps, two architectures, three scales each, and the effect survives at every LR. LLaMA-60M (n_embd 512, 8 layers) is architecturally almost identical to our model, and its 1.0B-token budget is the closest horizon here. Docked from 4 because (a) at OUR closest configuration the gain is smallest, 0.38 ppl ~ 0.015 nats, which is only just above our noise floor, (b) gains grow with scale and NS-step scarcity, both of which point away from us, (c) no seeds anywhere, and (d) it costs one extra full-size optimizer state buffer per matrix, plus an elementwise pass per step.
statement: Normalizing the momentum elementwise by an Adam-style second moment of the raw gradient BEFORE the Newton-Schulz iteration lowered validation perplexity versus plain Muon at matched Newton-Schulz step counts, consistently across six model configurations with the learning rate swept for both methods.

comparator: plain Muon at Ns=3 and Ns=5, both LR-swept, same FineWeb/C4 pre-training pipelines
effect: GPT-Small: Ns=3 preconditioned 28.12 vs Ns=5 plain Muon 29.51; GPT-Base 20.39 vs 21.47; GPT-Large 16.99 vs 17.56; plain Muon degrades sharply from Ns=5 to Ns=3 (29.51 -> 32.70 on GPT-Small) while the preconditioned version barely moves
locator: section 4.1 Table 1; section 3.5 'Overall Benefits'; Figure 3 (cosine similarity vs NS steps)
notes: transfer=3: normally this would be a double win (quality + throughput), but at 524288 tokens/step the Newton-Schulz cost is already amortized to near-nothing (2505.02222, overhead ~Theta(m/B)), so for US the NS-step saving is worth approximately zero wall-clock and only the quality half matters. Also note the tension with 2502.16982, which found NS=10 no better than NS=5: taken together, 5 is a plateau for plain Muon and preconditioning moves the plateau left, it does not raise it much. The extra second-moment buffer and elementwise division are the real cost on our budget.
statement: With second-moment preconditioning before orthogonalization, 3 Newton-Schulz steps outperformed plain Muon at 5 Newton-Schulz steps at all three GPT scales, i.e. a 40% reduction in orthogonalization iterations at better loss.

comparator: exact second-moment version and plain Muon under the same LR sweeps and pre-training budgets
effect: GPT-Small Ns=5: 27.93 (factorized) vs 27.95 (full) vs 29.51 (Muon); GPT-Base Ns=5: 20.58 vs 19.96 vs 21.47 (factorization loses ~0.6 ppl here); LLaMA scales show a gap of <=0.05 ppl
locator: section 3.6 Algorithm 2 (Muon2-F); section 4.1 Table 1 and section 4.2 Table 2
notes: transfer=3: the rationale is sound and matters for us -- the second moment only conditions the INPUT to orthogonalization, not the update itself, so it does not need to be exact. Two row/column vectors instead of a full matrix per parameter is cheap in both memory and elementwise traffic, which is the right shape for a throughput-constrained run. Caveat: the factorization is not uniformly harmless (GPT-Base loses 0.62 ppl of the 1.51 ppl gain), so if we adopt the preconditioner we should test full vs factorized rather than assume equivalence. No seeds.
statement: Replacing the full second-moment matrix with an Adafactor-style rank-one row/column factorization retained most of the benefit while leaving memory essentially unchanged from Muon.

comparator: plain Muon and the input-side preconditioned variant, all with swept hyperparameters, GPT-Small and GPT-Base on FineWeb
effect: GPT-Base: AdaMuon 26.07 (Ns=3) and 22.42 (Ns=5) vs plain Muon 24.69 and 21.47 -- i.e. AdaMuon LOST to Muon by 1.38 and 0.95 ppl; GPT-Small: AdaMuon 31.20/29.30 vs Muon 32.70/29.51 (marginally better); polar-side variants PolarExpress and Turbo-Muon also trailed
locator: section 4.3.2 and Table 3; Appendix C.3 Table 14 (AdaMuon LR sweep)
notes: transfer=3: this is a direct, hyperparameter-swept contradiction of 2507.11005's headline claim that AdaMuon dominates Muon, and it comes from a third party with per-method LR sweeps. Registered as opposing evidence so the controller does not treat AdaMuon as settled. The consistent story across 2604.09967, 2601.14603 and 2507.11005's own ablation is positional: elementwise adaptivity BEFORE Newton-Schulz helps, AFTER it is unreliable and can be worse than doing nothing. Both papers are single-run, so the disagreement may itself be noise -- which is a reason to spend at most one experiment slot here, on the pre-NS placement only.
statement: Muon variants that place the second moment on the Newton-Schulz OUTPUT (AdaMuon, NorMuon) underperformed input-side preconditioning at every tested setting and failed to reduce the required Newton-Schulz iterations; AdaMuon was worse than plain Muon on GPT-Base at both iteration counts.

comparator: Muon with the fused QKV projection treated as a single matrix for Newton-Schulz, Qwen-3-30B-A3B MoE, 24-25M-token batches, 1T tokens.
effect: Lower training loss early in the run; identical final loss at 1T tokens. No numeric gap is reported, only the loss curves in Figure 9.
locator: Appendix D.1 and Figure 9 (Qwen-3-30B-A3B); also section 5.5 where split-QKV is disabled for the Muon-vs-SOAP comparison
notes: Transfer 3 because a 600-1000 step run lives entirely inside the 'early in pretraining' window where the paper says the split helps, and the change is a few lines in the Muon param-grouping in train.py with negligible throughput cost (three smaller NS iterations instead of one large one). Scored down from 4 because the demonstration is at 30B params, the effect is only shown as a curve with no number, single run per arm, and the authors' own headline reading is that the difference is transient. Blocker: our fused-QKV layout must actually be fused for this to be a lever at all.
statement: Splitting the fused QKV tensor into separate Q, K, V matrices before Newton-Schulz orthogonalization in Muon lowers training loss early in pretraining, with the gap closing by the end of a 1T-token horizon.

comparator: Muon/SOAP with Nesterov-style momentum vs plain EMA momentum, 8B dense to 72B MoE, 1T-3T tokens, 25M-token batches.
effect: No observed convergence improvement; the authors dropped Nesterov and used a plain EMA with beta1=0.9 for all reported runs.
locator: section 5.2 (Optimizer Comparison Protocol), final paragraph; Algorithm 1 line 4 uses a plain EMA
notes: Transfer 2: the knob is a one-line flag in any Muon implementation and momentum handling is scale-generic, but the observation is at 8B-72B params over trillions of tokens, whereas Nesterov's usual justification (Keller Jordan's original Muon post, and 2511.06086 section II which reports the opposite) is at small scale and short horizon. Internal validity 1: this is an unquantified aside with no ablation figure, no seeds, and no loss numbers. Direct conflict with 2511.06086's restatement that Nesterov is empirically better makes this worth registering as contested rather than settled.
statement: Using Nesterov momentum instead of a plain exponential moving average for the momentum buffer did not improve convergence for either Muon or SOAP in the authors' large-batch pretraining runs.

comparator: Muon at 2x and 3x the 25M-token global batch vs the AdamW 25M-token baseline, 30B-A3B hybrid MoE, 3T tokens.
effect: Relative loss gap vs the AdamW 25M-token baseline is positive (worse) early and crosses over later; the inset plots the gap as a function of tokens. No crossover step count is given.
locator: Figure 1 caption and section 5.3 (NVIDIA-Nemotron-Nano-V3 30B-A3B, 3T tokens); Figure 3 batch-size ramp-up schedules
notes: Transfer 2: the qualitative shape (bigger batch is a late-horizon bet, and the price is paid early) is exactly the regime our 600-1000-step run sits in, and it argues against trading step count for batch size. But it is demonstrated at 30B params on a 3T-token horizon with MoE routing effects (section 3.1) that do not exist for us, and our batch is fixed by the frozen loader anyway, so the claim is mostly a caution rather than an actionable lever. Single run per batch size, no seeds.
statement: Increasing global batch size (2x and 3x over a 25M-token baseline) makes loss worse than the smaller-batch baseline for the earlier part of the token horizon, and only catches up or overtakes as the token horizon scales.

comparator: Muon with 16-iteration PolarExpress Newton-Schulz, same update-RMS matching, same TP mode, non-split QKV, 30B-A3B MoE at 24M-token batch.
effect: Both SOAP and MOP show 'slightly lower' loss than the Muon baseline throughout most of pretraining; magnitude shown only as a relative-difference inset, no number stated.
locator: section 5.5 and Figure 8 (Qwen-3-30B-A3B, global batch fixed at 24M tokens)
notes: Transfer 2: orthogonalization accuracy is a scale-generic property of the update rule and the campaign's host is input-pipeline bound so extra GPU FLOPs are comparatively cheap, making an exact-SVD or higher-iteration NS variant affordable in a way it usually is not. Held at 2, not 3, because the only evidence is a 30B MoE curve with no numeric effect size, no seeds, and because per-step SVD on 512-wide matrices still adds a CPU-synchronizing op that could cost steps. KL-SOAP itself is out of scope (memory footprint and eigenbasis recomputation every step).
statement: Replacing Muon's Newton-Schulz orthogonalization with an exact polar decomposition via SVD (MOP), and likewise KL-SOAP, yields slightly lower cross-entropy loss than Newton-Schulz Muon under update-RMS matching.

comparator: AdamW at constant LR (best config: beta=(0.9,0.95), LR 1e-3) vs SF-AdamW at constant LR (best config: beta=(0.95,0.99), LR 2e-3), both grid-searched, 124M LLaMA-style, SlimPajama-6B, 0.5M-token batch, 5000 steps.
effect: Decay phase (linear 1e-4 to 0) applied at SF-AdamW checkpoints gives minimal further loss reduction; the same procedure on the AdamW trajectory gives a sharp drop. Effect is shown as curves, no delta stated.
locator: section 3 ('Vanishing Benefit of Learning Rate Decay and Weight Averaging' and 'Schedule-Free Optimizer Tracks the River'), Figure 2 and Figure 3; replicated on OpenWebText2 in Figure 10
notes: Transfer 3: this is the closest operating point in the whole batch (124M params, 0.5M-token batch, GPT-2 tokenizer, no data-pipeline change, SF-AdamW is a drop-in optimizer swap). Held below 4 because it is 5000 steps / ~2.5B tokens (1x Chinchilla) versus our ~600-1000 steps / ~0.3-0.5B tokens, and the entire river-valley argument is about reaching a regime our run may never enter; a schedule-free method's advantage is that it does not need a horizon, which is worth little when our horizon is known and fixed. Also: our optimizer is a Muon+AdamW hybrid, and SF has not been composed with Muon here. Single seed per config; gradient clipping was disabled for SF-AdamW, which is a confound.
statement: At 124M parameters with a 0.5M-token batch, SF-AdamW trained at a constant learning rate reaches near-optimal loss on its own: applying a subsequent LR decay phase or an EWA of iterates yields no additional benefit, whereas the same decay phase produces a sharp loss drop for AdamW.

comparator: SF-AdamW at its tuned beta1=0.95 on the same 124M / 0.5M-token-batch / 5000-step SlimPajama setup.
effect: 2.7x worse perplexity (25.12 -> 67.20) moving beta1 from 0.95 to 0.1; the paper attributes the failure to x_t no longer tracking the river when beta1 is small.
locator: Appendix C.1, Table 5 (SlimPajama, 0.5M-token batch, 124M model, LR 2e-3, beta2=0.99); mechanism in section 3 'Sensitivity to Momentum Parameters' and Figure 4
notes: Transfer 3: same param count and batch size as our target, and the failure mode is a single hyperparameter we would have to get right on the first try. This is the main risk gate on adopting schedule-free at all: an untuned beta1 does not cost a few thousandths of bpb, it costs a factor. Not 4 only because the horizon is 5x ours and perplexity was measured on 9M held-out tokens at 2.5B tokens trained, so the ordering at 600 steps is unverified. Single seed per cell.
statement: Vanilla SF-AdamW is extremely sensitive to the momentum parameter beta1: test perplexity degrades from 25.12 at beta1=0.95 to 27.70 at 0.9, 41.01 at 0.5 and 67.20 at 0.1, all at the same LR of 2e-3.

comparator: Vanilla SF-AdamW (C = 1/(1-beta1)) at the same LR 2e-3, beta2=0.99, 124M LLaMA-style, SlimPajama-6B, 0.5M-token batch, 5000 steps.
effect: -1.52 perplexity (-6.1% relative) at beta1=0.95; -3.73 (-13.5%) at beta1=0.9. Gains persist for all of C in {50,100,200,500} at beta1=0.9 and 0.95, and C in {50,100} improves every momentum value tested.
locator: section 5 ('Our Refined SF Method', 'Empirical gains') and Appendix C.1 Table 5 (0.5M-token batch); Table 6 for the 2M-token batch
notes: Transfer 3: 124M / 0.5M-token batch is our operating point, the change is a scalar in the optimizer step, and the reported robustness to C (a whole order of magnitude works) is exactly what a campaign that cannot afford a sweep needs. Held below 4 because the run is 5000 steps and, critically, alpha_t ~ (C/T)(t/T)^(C-1) means the averaging window is defined relative to total steps T; with T~600 a C of 100-200 concentrates almost all weight on the last handful of iterates, so the tuned C does not carry over unchanged. Single seed per cell; these are the authors' own 'preliminary experiments'.
statement: Decoupling the averaging window from momentum in schedule-free AdamW by introducing c_t=(1-beta)C/t lowers test perplexity over vanilla SF-AdamW across a wide range of C at 124M scale: 25.12 -> 23.60 at beta1=0.95 (C=100) and 27.70 -> 23.97 at beta1=0.9 (C=50).

comparator: AdamW with cosine LR decay to 10% of peak, 124M model, 2M-token batch, 2500 steps (~5B tokens, ~2x Chinchilla).
effect: Vanilla SF-AdamW final loss is above AdamW+cosine at 2M-token batch; refined SF with C=200 matches (not beats) it. Table 6: vanilla beta1=0.98 gives 26.09 ppl, C=1000 gives 23.88.
locator: section 5 'Empirical gains' third bullet and Figure 9-right; Appendix C.1 Table 6; limitation restated in section 2.4
notes: Transfer 3 and registered as opposing evidence deliberately: the campaign's step budget is short and its batch is large for the model size, which is the direction in which SF is documented to degrade (the paper cites Zhang et al. and Morwani et al. for the same). This is the strongest single argument against swapping in schedule-free at our operating point without also tuning C. Scored 3 not 4 because 2M tokens/step is 4x our batch and 2500 steps is still 3-4x our horizon; single seed.
statement: At a 2M-token batch size, vanilla SF-AdamW with its best momentum (beta1=0.98) underperforms AdamW with a cosine schedule, and only matches it after adding the refinement parameter C=200.

comparator: Each other, after a per-scheme learning-rate sweep; LLaMA 20 blocks, d_emb 2048, ~1B params, DCLM 10% subset, 20,000 steps at 2^20 tokens/step, bf16, lambda=0.1.
effect: Best losses 2.815 (no WD) / 2.801 (independent WD) / 2.798 (standard WD); max spread 0.017 nats. The large differences between schemes appear only in how well the optimal LR transfers across widths, not in the achievable loss at one width.
locator: Appendix F.3.1 (Details for Figure 1), reporting best losses for the width-2048 / ~1B-param LLaMA runs on DCLM, 20B tokens
notes: Transfer 2 and registered as opposing evidence: our campaign never changes width, so the entire muP/LR-transfer payload is inapplicable, and this appendix number says the weight-decay scheme is worth ~0.01 nats at a fixed width once the LR is retuned - below or near our noise band. It argues against spending runs on weight-decay bookkeeping. Not scored higher because it is 1B params over 20B tokens / 20k steps (~30x our step budget) and the losses are averages of the last 100 training steps, not a clean held-out eval; also the input-layer/gain LRs were frozen at different values per arm, which is a confound between the no-WD and WD rows.
statement: At a single fixed model width, the best-over-learning-rate final loss is nearly identical whether AdamW uses no weight decay (2.815), independent weight decay scaling (2.801) or standard weight decay scaling (2.798) - a spread of at most 0.017 nats.

comparator: The steady-state theory of Kosson et al. that the relative update size depends only on eta*lambda, which the paper reformulates and then bounds in time.
effect: T_EQ ~ (1/(2*eta*lambda)) * ln(...); at eta=8e-3, lambda=0.1 the prefactor alone is 625 steps, so a few-hundred-step run never reaches the steady state in which only the product eta*lambda matters.
locator: Appendix D.1, Equation 31 (rho_inf^2 = eta/(2*lambda)) and Equation 32 (T_EQ); parameters eta=8e-3, lambda=0.1 from Appendix F.3
notes: Transfer 3: this is an analytic result parameterized directly by our own eta and lambda, and it says something the campaign can act on - in a 600-1000-step run weight decay is operating almost entirely in its transient regime, so it behaves as an initial-update scaler / implicit warmup (Appendix D.3) rather than as a norm regulator, and lambda should be tuned as a warmup-shaping knob and not by steady-state reasoning. Internal validity 2 because the authors explicitly state (Appendix D.1) that Equation 28 'does not accurately predict the behavior of the weight norm in neural network training' and that the model overestimates time-to-equilibrium; treat T_EQ as an order of magnitude, not a number. Also derived for AdamW, not Muon.
statement: The number of steps for AdamW weight norms to come within a factor sqrt(2) of their weight-decay equilibrium scales as 1/(2*eta*lambda) times a logarithmic factor, so with typical eta*lambda ~ 8e-4 equilibrium is an O(10^3)-step phenomenon.

comparator: LLaMA training at widths 128-2048, AdamW, 20k steps at 2^20 tokens/step, 10% linear warmup + linear decay baseline, best-LR sweep per arm.
effect: With no muP scaling, 10% and 50% linear warmup both give poor LR transfer; adding the multiplicative factor m^min(0, t/T_W - 1) or the decay-away factor of Equation 13 recovers transfer quality comparable to muP+independent WD, though it 'can require tuning and is less stable at higher learning rates'.
locator: section 6 ('The warmup effect of muP with independent weight decay') and section 7 with Figure 6 (three panels) and Figure 7; warmup forms in Equations 12 and 13
notes: Transfer 2: the width-transfer motivation is irrelevant to a fixed-width campaign, but the extractable mechanism - that warmup SHAPE (exponential, starting ~1/m below peak) matters more than warmup LENGTH, and that long linear warmup is not a substitute - is a cheap schedule change in train.py. Held at 2 because every experiment is a cross-width LR-transfer plot at 20k steps; there is no evidence at all that exponential warmup lowers loss at a single width and a short horizon, and burning warmup on a 600-step run costs a large fraction of the budget. Losses are last-100-step training averages.
statement: The practical benefit of muP's learning-rate scaling in AdamW is an implicit warmup effect on the relative weight updates, and an explicit additional exponential-shaped warmup factor can reproduce good learning-rate transfer without muP, whereas simply lengthening linear warmup from 10% to 50% of training does not.

comparator: None run. The paper's own AdamW alignment measurements (Figure 4, section 5.1) are the implicit contrast.
effect: No measurement. Stated as an expectation ('could result in', 'could potentially explain'); every experiment in the paper uses AdamW.
locator: section 9 (Discussion & Conclusion), final paragraph on matrix-level optimizers
notes: Transfer 2 because the campaign already runs a Muon+AdamW hybrid and 'shorten or drop warmup on the Muon-owned parameter group' is a zero-cost knob that buys back steps at the front of a 600-step run - but internal validity 1: this is an unsupported conjecture in a discussion section with no Muon run anywhere in the paper. Register it as a hypothesis to test cheaply, not as evidence. If tested, the AdamW-owned groups (embeddings, gains, 1-D params) may still need their warmup.
statement: The authors conjecture that matrix-level optimizers such as Muon produce a constant, low update alignment that does not vary over training, which would explain Muon's reduced need for learning-rate warmup and bypass the alignment dynamics that muP and weight decay are compensating for.

comparator: Best decay-based scheduler per model (WSD alpha=0.0 at 1B; Linear alpha=0.0 at 8B), AdamW, FineWeb-Edu, 80,000 steps, 4.2M (1B) / 12.6M (8B) token batches, eta_max=3e-4, 1000 warmup steps, WSD stable ratio 0.75.
effect: +0.071 nats (1B, 350B tokens) and +0.127 nats (8B, 500B tokens) validation loss relative to the best decay-based scheduler; the same models are best after SFT, but that inversion is irrelevant to a pretraining-loss objective.

comparator: One-sample SGD (B=1), which the theorem recovers as a special case; and multi-pass batch SGD with/without replacement.

Verified empirically only on synthetic Gaussian-sketched data (d=1e4, M=64, N=L=512, 100 repetitions).
locator: section 3, Theorem 3.1 and the discussion paragraphs 'What batch size changes' and 'Implications for choosing batch size'; empirical check in section 4 Experiment 1 and Figure 1(a)
notes: Transfer 1 - this does not transfer and I am saying so plainly. It is sketched linear regression with a power-law covariance spectrum and a source condition, plain SGD with no momentum, no adaptivity, no features; the authors themselves list extension to nonlinear or feature-learning models as open. The only reason to register it at all is that the one-pass structure literally matches our single-epoch-over-a-fixed-shard-set regime and the conclusion (batch size is a noise-control knob whose benefit saturates, and buying it with horizon is a bad trade when the bias term dominates) points the same way as 2607.20548's Figure 1. Do not use it as evidence for a batch-size decision; it is a framing, not a measurement.
statement: In one-pass (single-epoch) batch SGD the 1/B variance gain from a larger batch is partly cancelled at a fixed dataset size by the shorter optimization horizon T=N/B, so batch size should be increased only until the variance term stops being comparable to the approximation-plus-bias contribution.

comparator: Dynamic Tanh (Zhu et al. 2025), fitted on the same simulated LayerNorm outlier data. No neural network is trained anywhere in the paper.

notes: Transfer 1 and I am saying so plainly: there is not a single training run in this paper. The 'simulations' are a curve fit of two functional forms to synthetic Gaussian data passed through LayerNorm, and the authors explicitly leave 'how ELN compares to DyT in terms of performance and feasibility' to future work. The usual motivation for DyT-style replacements is throughput (no cross-channel reduction), and per this campaign's own finding that ~94% of charged time is the frozen Python packing loop, a faster normalization op buys close to nothing in wall clock here - so even the speed argument does not land at our operating point. statement: Elementwise Layer Normalization, y = sqrt(C-1) * x / sqrt(beta + x^2), is the exact element-wise solution of the LayerNorm differential equation of which Dynamic Tanh is an approximation, and it reproduces LayerNorm's response to outliers far more closely than DyT in a synthetic fit.

It is direct evidence against spending a slot on inverse-sqrt base schedules. Also the entire motivation (post-hoc horizon extension without re-tuning) is irrelevant when our horizon is fixed at 300 charged seconds.
statement: An inverse-square-root base phase (WSqD) only MATCHES flat-stable WSD at the shortest horizon tested and its advantage grows with horizon, at both 124M and 213M params.

comparator: same schedule, same LR 0.0015, three independent (init, data-shuffle) seed pairs, 213M LLaMA on SlimPajama

Practical consequence: any lever whose claimed effect is a few thousandths of a nat needs n>=3 and sign-consistency across seeds, exactly as they did, or it should not be believed. Docked from 4 only because the measurement is at 213M and 15k-60k iterations, and seed noise typically grows at shorter horizons.

comparator: per-horizon grid over six peak LRs, 213M LLaMA on SlimPajama, AdamW, decay fraction 0.2, 300-step warmup

Not 4 because the horizons swept (15k-60k) are all far above ours and the drift is only demonstrated for AdamW with WSD, not for a Muon+AdamW hybrid.
statement: The optimal peak learning rate for a WSD schedule drifts toward SMALLER values as the training horizon grows, whereas the horizon-free WSqD schedule's optimum stays fixed.

comparator: WSqD with T_0 in {500,5000,10000}, peak LR selected on a 10000-iteration search, 213M LLaMA on SlimPajama

That is a useful structural warning: at our horizon the schedule family degenerates. Evidence is 3 values of T_0, one seed, at 213M.

comparator: Adam and Muon with grid-searched LR, no weight decay, momentum 0.95

The modification itself is cheap (one extra accumulated scalar, no extra tensor state, no extra Newton-Schulz) and would be trivially implementable in train.py, but there is zero evidence at any language-model scale, the optimal LR moves by 2 orders of magnitude (Muon 5e-3 -> AdaGO 0.5 on regression), and it introduces two new hyperparameters (epsilon, gamma) we cannot afford to sweep. Not usable without our own screening run.

comparator: per-optimizer best configuration tuned at the near-Chinchilla 2.1B-token horizon, then lambda swept over {0, 0.1, 0.5}; Llama-like 124M, FineWeb 100B subset, GPT-2 tokenizer, seqlen 512, batch 256x512=131k tokens, cosine to 0.01*gamma_max

locator: section 4.1 'Weight decay ablation', Figure 7(a,b); appendix D.1 'Weight decay ablation', Figure 23
notes: Transfer 3 and this is the single most on-point lever in the batch: same parameter count, same data family, same tokenizer, and the effect is explicitly a SHORT-HORIZON effect that reverses with more tokens. Docked from 4 because their shortest run (1B tokens = 8k iterations at this batch) is still ~10x our step budget, so the monotone trend has to be extrapolated one further decade toward us; the direction of extrapolation, however, is favorable. Study is unusually strong internally: 2900 models, ~30000 GPU-hours, per-optimizer tuning. Blocker: see the Muon-specific exception.
statement: At 124M params, holding the tuned learning rate fixed and raising decoupled weight decay from 0.1 to 0.5 gives better final validation loss for short training durations, with lambda=0.1 only overtaking it at the longest horizon.

comparator: same 124M setup and the same {0, 0.1, 0.5} sweep applied to D-Muon, where weight decay reaches all parameter groups and the normal 'large lambda for short runs' pattern reappears

locator: appendix D.1 'Weight decay ablation' (text) and Figure 23; section 4.1 Figure 8
notes: Transfer 3 and this is the critical caveat for us because we run a Muon+AdamW hybrid: raising the weight decay hyperparameter is only a short-horizon win if the decay actually reaches the matrix parameters. If our Muon path excludes 2D params from decay, cranking lambda will load all the regularization onto the AdamW-owned groups (embeddings, norms, head) and can hurt. Same horizon caveat as the parent claim.
statement: For plain Muon, which does not apply weight decay to its 2D matrix parameters, lambda=0.5 UNDERPERFORMS lambda in {0, 0.1} even on the short training runs where large weight decay helps every other optimizer.

comparator: basic Muon (jordan2024muon) with weight decay only on embeddings, scalar params and the final layer, same tuning protocol, 124M/210M/720M Llama-like models on FineWeb
effect: major improvement of D-Muon over Muon at all three model sizes; basic Muon degrades further as model size grows while D-Muon is consistent across every setting tried; D-Muon's tuned LR at 124M large-batch is 0.002 vs Muon's 0.01 Muon-LR/0.001 AdamW-LR split
locator: section 4.1 Figure 8(a,b,c) and section 3 Figure 4; 720M discussion in section 4.3
notes: Transfer 3: a concrete, cheap, implementable change to the Muon path (decay the 2D matrices too, share the LR treatment) validated at exactly our parameter count on FineWeb data. Docked from 4 because every horizon tested is >=8k iterations and because the comparison also bundles a learning-rate parameterization change alongside the weight-decay change, so the attribution to weight decay alone rests on the authors' cross-reference to Figures 7 and 23 rather than an isolated A/B.
statement: D-Muon, which applies decoupled weight decay to all parameter groups including the 2D matrices, substantially outperforms basic Muon at 124M, 210M and 720M params, and the gap is attributed to the weight decay.

comparator: AdamW at 124M and 210M with the same peak LR and schedule shape, sweeping gamma_end over 1e-1 to 1e-6 times gamma_max
effect: decaying only to 0.1*gamma_max is much worse than any deeper decay tested; best endpoint at 210M is 0.01*gamma_max for cosine and WSD and 0.001*gamma_max for linear; at 124M the best shifts further to 1e-4*gamma_max for linear and 1e-6*gamma_max for WSD; differences beyond 0.1x are described as relatively small

Docked from 4 because horizons are 8k-128k iterations; at 600-1000 steps the decay phase is a much larger fraction of the run, so the endpoint interacts with the schedule shape differently, and the authors themselves note the gains beyond 0.1x are 'relatively small'.
statement: Decaying the learning rate to 0.01x the peak or lower gives significantly better final loss than the common 0.1x endpoint, at both 124M and 210M params.

comparator: Muon at 124M, batch 256x512=131k tokens, 16k steps, otherwise best-found configuration

notes: Transfer 4: demonstrated at exactly 124M with a FineWeb-tokenized GPT-2-vocabulary setup, implementable as a one-line change, and it is a pure throughput lever - in our CPU-contended, launch-bound regime every removed NS iteration is removed kernel launches per matrix per step, which converts directly into steps. The one gap: they do not report whether T_NS=1 is as good as 5 (the sweep includes 1 but the text only states 'beyond 5 does not improve'), so the downside direction is unverified and worth screening ourselves at n=1 on step count.
statement: Increasing Muon's Newton-Schulz iteration count beyond 5 does not improve final loss and only costs wall-clock time.

comparator: each optimizer's own best 16.8B-token configuration with only T_warmup varied; 124M Llama-like on FineWeb, batch 256x512

locator: section 4.1 'Warmup ablation', Figure 10; appendix D.1 'Warmup ablation', Figure 22
notes: Transfer 3: the DIRECTION (small warmup fraction, and optimizer-dependent) transfers; the absolute count does not - 1.56% of our 600-1000 steps is only ~10-16 steps, well below anything they tested, so the linear extrapolation is unsafe and we should treat this as 'sweep warmup low, and expect the answer to differ between the Muon-owned and AdamW-owned parameter groups'. Sweep had only 3 (for AdamW, 5) points and one seed per point.
statement: At 124M params a short warmup of about 1.5% of total iterations was best for most optimizers, and the published recommendation of warming up over 25% of the Chinchilla-optimal duration was clearly worse.

comparator: identical OLMo2 baselines with RMSNorm, identical corpus (OLMo-mix-1124), same token budgets
effect: c4_en validation loss 3.011 -> 3.008 for OLMo2-550M at 400B tokens and 2.884 -> 2.879 for OLMo2-1B at 500B tokens; the MoE gain is larger (2.922 -> 2.900 at 1.3B/500B) and the authors attribute the dense shortfall to dense parameters already being sufficiently trained
locator: section 4.1 'Dense Models' and Table 1 (OLMo2-550M and OLMo2-1B rows)
notes: Transfer 1 and stance OPPOSES: every number in this paper comes from 400B-1000B token runs, the dense-model effect is 0.003-0.005 nats there, and the authors explicitly report the advantage GROWING with tokens - so the expected effect at 0.3-0.5B tokens is at or below zero. It also adds a per-normalization-layer matvec (x . beta^T), a tanh and two extra learnable vectors at every norm site including QK-norm, which in our launch-bound step is a real throughput cost for no demonstrated short-horizon benefit.
statement: On DENSE language models SeeDNorm's validation-loss improvement over RMSNorm is a few thousandths of a nat and the authors state the training-loss improvement widens as the token count increases.

comparator: OLMoE-1.3B baseline with RMSNorm, all ablations trained for 500B tokens on OLMoE-mix-0924
effect: alpha initialized to 10 gives c4_en loss 3.154 versus 2.900 at alpha=1 and 2.912 at alpha=0.1 (baseline RMSNorm 2.922), i.e. a large-init gain is much worse than doing nothing; replacing tanh with GeLU or Swish makes the model fail to converge, while sigmoid, tanh and hardtanh all converge and beat the baseline
locator: section 4.3 'Initialization of alpha' and 'Activation Function in SeeDNorm', Figure 4 and Table 4
notes: Transfer 2: the transferable content is the guardrail, not the method - any lever that makes a normalization gain depend on the activations must bound the gain path (saturating nonlinearity) and start it small, or it destabilizes training. Docked heavily because all ablations are 500B-token MoE runs at 1.3B params, n=1 per cell, and the sensitivity ordering could differ at 600 steps where the gain parameters have barely moved from init.
statement: For an input-dependent normalization gain, the initialization of the rescaling magnitude is stability-critical and an unbounded activation in the gain path prevents convergence entirely.

comparator: OLMoE-1.3B with RMSNorm, 500B tokens, identical corpus and hyperparameters
effect: c4_en loss 2.968 vs 2.922 baseline and PPL 19.45 vs 18.63; all five downstream accuracies drop (ARC-C 30.4 vs 32.3, ARC-E 61.9 vs 62.2, HellaSwag 53.2 vs 55.2, MMLU-Var 30.5 vs 32.4, PIQA 70.6 vs 72.6)

notes: Transfer 2: relevant only as opposing evidence against the tempting throughput lever of deleting RMSNorm's reduction (a real cost in a launch-bound step) in favor of a pointwise saturating activation. Not higher because it is a 500B-token MoE result at 1.3B params with n=1 and the ranking could plausibly differ in a 600-step run where normalization is doing more of the early conditioning work, not less.
statement: Replacing RMSNorm with DyT, a saturating activation that removes the normalization statistics, slows convergence and degrades both validation loss and every downstream task on a language model.

comparator: full-precision full-memory training of the same LLaMA models on C4 without data repetition, seqlen 256, global batch 512, LR tuned per model size, linear warmup 10% then cosine to 10% of peak; 10K/60K/100K steps for 60M/350M/1B
