locator: appendix A, Table 2 (pretraining perplexity by model size and compression ratio); section 4.2
notes: Transfer 2 and stance OPPOSES: the only data point near our capacity (60M, 10K steps) shows a consistent DEGRADATION that worsens monotonically with compression, and the paper's headline 'quality preserved or improved' rests entirely on the 350M and 1B runs. This is a scale-dependence warning for any sequence-dimension activation approximation in the attention input path: the redundancy the method exploits appears not to be there yet at small capacity. n=1 per cell, perplexity only.
statement: Approximating the QKV projection weight gradients by compressing the saved input activations along the sequence dimension degrades perplexity at 60M params while improving it at 350M and 1B.

comparator: full-memory training on A100s; FlashAttention-v2 used throughout and the output projection deliberately left untouched to avoid perturbing gradients into FlashAttention
effect: QKV projection activation memory reduced up to 512x (LLaMA-1B: 3 GB -> 18 MB), which the authors note is ~20% of attention-block peak memory; all PAMM-trained weights use a reduced rate eta_tilde = 0.25 * eta 'for stability'; authors state implementing PAMM in CUDA to achieve its theoretical speedup is a future direction
locator: section 6 'Conclusion' (CUDA implementation listed as future work), appendix A (learning-rate scaling alpha=0.25), section 5 'Limitations'
notes: Transfer 0: memory is not a binding constraint for a 124M model on an H200, and the intervention as published adds Python/PyTorch-level compression work per layer per step with no fused kernel, which in our CPU-contended, launch-bound regime costs steps and therefore costs val_bpb. The forced 4x learning-rate reduction on those weights is an additional disqualifier at a 600-step horizon where every step of effective learning rate counts.
statement: The QKV activation compression method delivers activation-memory savings only; no wall-clock speedup is demonstrated and it requires a reduced learning rate on the affected weights for stability.

comparator: No trained baseline: this is the argmin of the RHS of a published LMO convergence bound (eq. 2) with all constants C_1=C_2=C_3=1. The only empirical support is a 160M PlainLM on <=5B SlimPajama tokens.
effect: eta*_T(b) proportional to b^{1/2} T^{-1/2}; practical rule eta_1 = eta_0 (T_0/T_1)^{1/2} when b and momentum are held fixed
locator: Theorem 1 (section 3.1, eq. 6-7) and Appendix A Table 2 regime (A)
notes: Transfer 2, not higher: the derivation assumes a CONSTANT learning rate, no warmup, no weight decay, no schedule and matched initialization, so 'eta*' is not the same object as our peak LR under a warmup+cooldown schedule. It is also a large-horizon asymptotic and Figure 1 shows a burn-in phase before the trends hold, which is exactly the 600-1000-step regime we live in. Directly contradicted empirically by 2604.27077, which fits -1/3 and calls the -1/2 exponent 'too large'. No seeds or uncertainty anywhere; the numerical verification is a grid over the bound, not over training runs.
statement: For LMO-type optimizers (Muon, signSGD/Adam surrogates, normalized SGD), minimizing a convergence-bound proxy at fixed batch size and fixed momentum gives an optimal learning rate scaling as T^{-1/2} with token budget, i.e. the transfer rule eta_1 = eta_0 (T_0/T_1)^{1/2}.

comparator: Same proxy-bound minimization as above; no training run tests momentum scaling in this paper.
effect: risk_T proportional to alpha^{1/2} b_max^{-1/2} (non-vanishing) at fixed alpha; restored to T^{-1/4} by alpha*_T(b) proportional to b T^{-1/2}, i.e. beta = 1-alpha driven toward 1 as the horizon grows
locator: Corollary 1 part 2, section 3.2; Theorem 2 (eq. 8)
notes: Transfer 2. Our batch IS hardware-capped at 524288 tokens/step, so the capped regime is the one that applies, and this is the paper's one argument that momentum is a real (not cosmetic) knob for us. But it is a bound, not a measurement; the prescription is asymptotic in T while our T is small; and the direction it prescribes (raise beta as steps grow) is the opposite of what a 600-step run's short averaging window might want. Blocker: no empirical validation of momentum scaling at any scale in this work.
statement: When batch size is capped by hardware, tuning only the learning rate at a fixed momentum leaves a non-vanishing noise floor proportional to alpha^{1/2} b_max^{-1/2} in the LMO proxy bound, and letting the momentum parameter alpha decrease with the token budget removes that floor.

comparator: Proxy bound at optimally tuned (eta, b) for arbitrary fixed momentum vs optimally tuned momentum; no measured loss.
effect: risk*_T(alpha) proportional to (1+alpha)^{1/4} T^{-1/4}; best possible gain from re-tuning alpha is 1.19x in the rate constant
locator: Corollary 1 part 1, section 3.2
notes: Registered as opposing evidence against spending budget on momentum tuning. Transfer 2 with a caveat that cuts the other way: the corollary's premise (batch free to grow) is FALSE for us, and the companion corollary (previous claim) says momentum matters more under a batch cap. So this bounds the payoff only in the regime we are not in. It also bounds a rate constant of a loose upper bound, which need not track val_bpb at all. Use it as a prior against momentum-sweeping, not as proof.
statement: If batch size can be tuned freely, re-tuning momentum changes the LMO proxy's asymptotic rate constant by at most a factor 2^{1/4} (about 1.19), so momentum tuning is close to irrelevant in that regime.

comparator: 160M PlainLM on SlimPajama, Adam betas fixed (0.9,0.95), 8% warmup then constant LR, grid over eta at each of 3 batch sizes; baseline is the other grid points, not a separate recipe.
effect: At T=5B tokens: eta*=0.001 at b=32, 0.003 at b=128, 0.01 at b=512. At b=32: eta* shifts from 0.003 to 0.001 after 2.5B tokens; at b=128 the switch point is not reached by 5B tokens.
locator: Figure 3 (section 4), empirical support experiment
notes: Transfer 3: 160M is the closest parameter scale in this batch to our 124M, and the two directions are usable priors. But n=1 per grid point with no seeds or error bars, only 3 batch sizes, constant-LR (not our cooldown recipe), and the token budgets (2.5-5B) are 8-16x ours, so the 'decreases with horizon' half is measured entirely outside our horizon range and the switch point at b=128 was never even reached. The 'larger batch wants larger LR' half is the more usable one for us since our per-step batch is very large.
statement: In a 160M-parameter transformer grid search with 8% warmup and a constant learning rate, the best constant learning rate increased with batch size and decreased with token budget at fixed batch size.

comparator: WSD sweeps with cooldown fraction in {0,0.05,...,0.95}, peak rate tuned separately at every point, mean over 512 runs (8 for the deep linear net), against the same optimizer at cf=0.
effect: Cooldown gain (loss at cf=0 divided by best-cf loss) on the anisotropic quadratic: 1.0x for SGD, 1.7e6x for signSGD, 3.8e5x for normalized SGD; 5.8e6x for signSGD on a deep linear net. Measured floor exponent eta^{2.00+-0.01}; closed-form floor constant matches simulation within 0.7%.
locator: Proposition 2 and Remark 3 (section 4); Table 1 (section 5); Table 3 WSD sweeps (section 10)
notes: Internal validity 4 because the stationary law is solved exactly and simulation matches the closed form across the whole parameter range with >=1e5 post-burn-in steps and >=100 chains. Transfer only 2: every model is a quadratic, a quartic, a deep linear net or a 2-layer MLP -- there is no transformer and no language modelling anywhere. It matters to us only because Muon (spectral-norm normalized) and AdamW are both in the 'cannot self-anneal' class by the paper's criterion, which predicts our recipe genuinely needs decay to ~0. It gives no guidance on HOW to decay (see the interior-fraction claim).
statement: Under gradient-proportional (multiplicative) noise, sign-based and normalized updates sit on a last-iterate loss floor of order eta^2 that only driving the learning rate to zero removes, whereas plain SGD self-anneals and its optimal cooldown fraction is 0.

comparator: Two-layer ReLU 64-128-10 on scikit-learn digits (1500 images, minibatch 32), WSD sweep with peak rate tuned per point, 5 seeds, min-max bands, versus the same optimizer at cf=0.
effect: Adam cf*=0, ending 3.5x worse at strong cooldown; SGD cf*=0, 2.4x worse at cf=0.95; only signSGD improved (7.7e-2 to 6.6e-2). Adam's per-step update norm as a fraction of a full sign step fell from 0.33 to 0.02 while the gradient norm dropped 500x.
locator: Figure 2 and 'A real-data check' paragraph, section 10
notes: Registered as opposing evidence: it shows the 'normalized optimizers need cooldown' rule is not automatic for Adam. Transfer scored 1, not higher, because the workload is a 1500-image multi-epoch MLP sitting near interpolation, where the measured noise exponent is 0.56 and gradients collapse 500x; single-epoch 124M LM pretraining on FineWeb is nowhere near interpolation, gradients do not collapse like that, and the cooldown-helps result is empirically settled for LLM pretraining. Keep it visible as a mechanism warning (measure whether our Adam/Muon update norms are actually staying order-1 late in the run) rather than as a reason to cut cooldown.
statement: On the paper's one real-data workload, Adam's optimal cooldown fraction was 0 and strong cooldown made the final training loss 3.5x worse, because Adam's measured update magnitude shrank with the gradient instead of staying order-1.

comparator: Same WSD sweep protocol (cf grid of 20 values, peak rate tuned per point) within the same optimizer.
effect: Broad plateau over cooldown fraction in [0.4, 0.95] on the anisotropic quadratic and [0.8, 0.95] on the real-data signSGD run; the authors state the argmin within the plateau is not determined and Table 3 should be read for the cf=0 vs plateau contrast only.
locator: 'Dissociation across models' paragraph, section 10; Table 3 caption
notes: Transfer 2: usable as a prior that fine-grained cooldown-fraction sweeps are low-yield relative to the noise floor of our A/B harness, but demonstrated only on toy landscapes. The plateau shape may well be narrower on a real transformer. This is a reason NOT to spend runs on cooldown-fraction knob-tuning.
statement: For sign-based and normalized optimizers the optimal cooldown fraction sits on a broad plateau near full decay rather than at a sharp argmin.

comparator: The paper's own full WSD sweeps versus reported practice in LLM pretraining (cited refs 7, 15, 2).
effect: Every optimum found is either 0 (SGD, multiplicative noise) or maximal / a plateau near full decay (normalized methods, or any method under additive noise). Interior optima are attributed to non-stationarity, feature learning or finite-data effects, none of which the model contains.
locator: Section 11, 'Not the interior WSD fraction'
notes: Boundary claim, stated by the authors as an explicit limitation, which is why internal validity is high. Transfer 2 and the value is negative: it tells us not to import this line of theory to choose a cooldown fraction for our run, and that the mechanism explaining an interior optimum is not yet in any stationary model. Useful for pruning a whole class of proposed schedule interventions rather than for launching one.
statement: No model in this study -- across quadratic, quartic, deep linear and a real MLP workload, and across noise structures and optimizers -- produces an interior optimal cooldown fraction, so the roughly 0.2-0.35 fractions used in real pretraining lie outside stationary landscape-and-noise geometry.

comparator: Same BLaLM (mLSTM token mixer) architecture, BabyLM strict track (100M words, 10 epochs, context 512, effective batch 64), a SINGLE shared learning rate of 4e-4 for both optimizers, cosine decay with 10% warmup.

Transfer 2: this confirms the hybrid we ALREADY run rather than offering a new lever, the backbone is an mLSTM not softmax attention, and the regime is 10 epochs over 100M words rather than a single epoch over FineWeb. Value is confirmatory only; do not treat it as a proposal.

comparator: Base BLaLM (mLSTM) at a fixed LR of 4e-4 with Muon, same 10-epoch budget, best-checkpoint selection by downstream average.
effect: Validation perplexity 20.01 -> 12.37 (strict-small, 10M words) and 7.95 -> 6.48 (strict, 100M words); note the zero-shot average went DOWN in both tracks (37.27 -> 36.41 and 35.08 -> 34.57).
locator: Section 6.5 Experiment 5, Table 6 (row '- ShortConv')
notes: Internal validity 1: n=1 per configuration, LR frozen at 4e-4 for every arm, and the strict-small base at that LR (20.01) is anomalously worse than the same base model at every other LR in Table 5 (15.73-16.61), so the 20.01 -> 12.37 delta is largely against a broken baseline. Checkpoints were also selected on downstream average, not perplexity. Transfer 2: short convs on Q/K are cheap and implementable on our attention path, and our objective is perplexity-like so the downstream regression does not count against it here, but the mechanism was only ever shown to help a linear-attention (mLSTM) mixer where it supplies local mixing our sliding-window attention already provides. Costs a per-step conv, which is charged against step count.
statement: Adding depthwise 1D short convolutions on the query and key projections before the token mixer lowered validation perplexity in both BabyLM tracks.

comparator: Same BLaLM/Muon setup across LR values; the comparator is the other LR grid points.
effect: Strict-track validation perplexity 9.83 (2e-4), 8.46 (3e-4), 8.06 (4e-4), 7.74 (5e-4), 7.76 (6e-4), 7.64 (7e-4), 7.70 (5.5e-4); the downstream-average optimum sat at 5.5e-4, i.e. perplexity and downstream disagree about the best LR.
locator: Section 6.4 Experiment 4, Table 5 (strict track PPL column)
notes: Internal validity 1: n=1 per LR, and the strict-small column reports the identical perplexity 16.41 at three different LRs, which is a reporting or checkpoint-selection artifact that undermines the whole table. Transfer 2, direction only: it suggests that in a data-limited regime the perplexity-optimal LR can sit at or above the top of a conventional sweep, and it warns that selecting LR on a downstream metric picks a different point than selecting on perplexity -- relevant because our sole objective IS the perplexity-like metric. Do not import the absolute LR values: different optimizer scaling, different architecture, batch 64x512 tokens versus our 524288.
statement: In a Muon learning-rate sweep under a 100M-word 10-epoch budget, validation perplexity fell monotonically across the entire swept range from 2e-4 to 7e-4 without reaching an interior optimum.

comparator: Same LLaMA-architecture models, 6.6B-token Pile subset, single H200, bf16, cosine + 10% warmup, batch 130k tokens, 3 seeds averaged; the two arms differ only in which optimizer touches the embedding table.
effect: Test perplexity 192.7 / 117.8 / 98.84 at 270M / 0.6B / 1.3B for SinkGD applied to all 2D weights including embeddings, versus 34.30 / 32.85 / 28.71 for the identical method with AdamW retained on the embedding layer. Attributed to sparse, high-variance Zipfian embedding gradients; the authors note the failure persists even with the LR retuned.
locator: Section 2.3 and Figure 1 (motivating experiment); Table 2 rows 'SinkGD-Pure' vs 'SinkGD-Hybrid'
notes: Transfer 3, the highest in this batch for an optimizer claim: 270M is close to our 124M, the run is a single-H200 from-scratch pretrain, and the conclusion applies directly to our parameter-group split, where AdamW handles the token embedding and value-embedding tables while Muon handles matrices. It is strong evidence against any 'unify the optimizer across all 2D parameters' proposal, including extending Muon-style orthogonalization to the embedding or VE tables. Held below 4 because 6.6B tokens is >10x our token budget and the failing method (SinkGD) is not Muon, so the result is about stateless normalization generally rather than Muon specifically.
statement: Applying a stateless normalizing optimizer to the embedding matrix instead of keeping a stateful adaptive optimizer there is catastrophic for perplexity at every scale tested.

comparator: Same models, data, budget and 3-seed protocol as above; arms differ only in whether dense 2D weights get the sign rule or the normalizing rule.
effect: Test perplexity 116.0 / 179.0 / 216.0 at 270M / 0.6B / 1.3B for the sign rule applied to all parameters, versus 29.95 / 26.71 / 24.33 when dense 2D weights keep a matrix-aware normalizing rule. The pure-sign arm gets monotonically worse with scale.
locator: Table 2 row 'SAGE-Pure' vs 'SAGE-Hybrid'; section 4.1 Optimizers and Baselines
notes: Transfer 3: it supports keeping a matrix-aware rule (our Muon) on dense weights and is a clean prune of the 'replace Muon with a cheaper sign-based update to buy throughput' direction, which is otherwise attractive at a 300-second budget because Newton-Schulz costs FLOPs. 270M/single-H200 makes the scale credible. Held below 4 because the comparator normalizer is SinkGD, not Muon, and the token budget is 6.6B.
statement: Applying the sign-based update to dense 2D weights as well as embeddings, instead of a matrix-aware normalizing rule, is far worse than the hybrid and degrades further as model size grows.

comparator: AdamW and other baselines at 'the learning rates favored by their original works' plus a sanity check at larger LRs; SAGE and unpublished hybrids got a fresh grid search. Same 6.6B Pile tokens, 3 seeds.
effect: Test perplexity 29.95 vs 37.35 (270M), 26.71 vs 31.74 (0.6B), 24.33 vs 27.81 (1.3B) against AdamW; also beats Lion-Hybrid (32.10 / 28.73 / 28.40) and SinkGD-Hybrid (34.30 / 32.85 / 28.71).
locator: Table 2, section 4.2 'Performance at Scale'
notes: Internal validity only 2 despite 3 seeds: the baselines were not tuned on a matched grid, and Lion-on-everything (30.24 at 270M) beating AdamW (37.35) is a strong smell that the AdamW arm was under-tuned, which inflates every reported margin. Transfer 2: the paper NEVER compares against Muon and says so in its own Limitations, so the delta against our actual baseline is unmeasured; the dense-layer half is not a drop-in for us. Only the embedding-side mechanism is worth extracting, and see the LR-headroom claim for that.
statement: A hybrid using a normalizing rule on dense weights and a bounded sign-with-damper rule on embeddings and 1D parameters reached lower test perplexity than AdamW at every scale tested from 270M to 1.3B.

comparator: Lion-Hybrid with an identical structure and the same learning rates, same 270M-1.3B models and 6.6B-token budget.
effect: Grid over {1e-4, 2e-4, 5e-4, 1e-3, 2e-3}: Lion-Hybrid peaks at 1e-4 and 'collapses shortly after', the damped variant peaks at 1e-3. Figure 3 shows the damper is sparse -- most dimensions stay clipped at scale 1.0 and only a few high-variance dimensions are damped, with damping becoming sparser after the first ~500 steps.
locator: Section 4.4 'Learning Rate Tuning and Stability'; Lemma 3.2; Figure 3
notes: Transfer 2. The mechanism -- a cheap per-dimension bounded damper on the embedding/VE parameter group to buy learning-rate headroom -- is implementable in train.py at O(d) memory and negligible FLOPs, and higher usable LR is a plausible lever at 600-1000 steps. But the headroom was demonstrated against Lion, not against AdamW or Muon, so it is not established that our current embedding optimizer is the one leaving LR headroom on the table. No seed count is given for the LR grid, and the damper's benefit is entangled with the SinkGD dense-layer rescaling the paper says was 'critical for stability'.
statement: Bounding the per-dimension embedding update magnitude at 1.0 with an O(d) L1-EMA relative damper kept training stable at a roughly 10x higher learning rate than the undamped sign baseline, which collapsed just above its optimum.

comparator: LLaMA2-130M, C4, 10000 steps, global batch 512, sequence length 1024 (~5.2B tokens), bf16, 1000 warmup steps, cosine to 10%, weight decay 0.1, a SINGLE fixed learning rate of 1e-3 shared by all optimizers.
effect: Rate improves from O(T^{-1/4}) to Otilde(T^{-1/3}) (and from Otilde(T^{-1/2}) to Otilde(T^{-2/3}) under PL); on LLaMA2-130M / C4, Muon-VR2 gives a faster drop and lower final train and validation loss than AdamW, Muon-EMA and Muon-VR1. No numeric losses are reported.
locator: Theorem 4.3 and Table 1; section 5 'LLaMA2 on C4' and Figure 2
notes: Internal validity 2: the LM result is curves only with no numbers, no seed count and no per-optimizer LR tuning (the CIFAR-10 arm got 5 seeds and a 7-point LR grid; the LM arm got neither). Transfer 2: 130M and 12 layers is close to our scale, but 10000 steps and 5.2B tokens is 10x our horizon, and the entire proposition is about the asymptotic-T regime where a T^{-1/3} vs T^{-1/4} distinction can be read. See the paired throughput claim -- at a fixed 300s wall clock this variant is very likely net-negative.
statement: A two-batch variance-reduced Muon variant attains an Otilde(T^{-1/3}) ergodic rate, versus O(T^{-1/4}) for standard Muon, and reached lower training and validation loss than AdamW and both standard Muon variants on a 130M language model.

comparator: VR2 versus VR1/EMA on the same task, compared on wall-clock time rather than on step count.
effect: VR2 needs grad f(X_t; xi_t) and grad f(X_{t-1}; xi_t), i.e. two backward passes per optimizer step; the authors show the cost in wall-clock (Fig 1c) and call the overhead potentially prohibitive at scale, positioning VR1 as the pragmatic alternative with 'minimal degradation'.
locator: Section 3 (Option VR2, eq. 5, 'one gradient evaluation per step versus two'); Remark 5.1; Figure 1c (test accuracy vs wall-clock time)
notes: Registered as opposing evidence and scored transfer 3 because the objection bites hardest exactly at our operating point: our objective is val_bpb within 300 CHARGED SECONDS, so roughly doubling per-step gradient cost roughly halves step count, and step count dominates val_bpb at fixed wall clock. The per-iteration win in Figure 2 is measured against steps, not seconds; the authors' own wall-clock figure and Remark 5.1 are the honest reading. Their caveat that a larger batch mitigates the noise VR2 targets also applies to us, since our per-step batch is already 524288 tokens.
statement: The variance-reduced Muon variant that achieves the improved rate requires two gradient evaluations per step, and the authors state its computational overhead can be prohibitive and recommend the one-gradient approximation when compute efficiency is the priority.

comparator: Worst-case rates under identical L-smoothness, unbiased-gradient and bounded-variance assumptions; not a training comparison.
effect: Muon-EMA: O(T^{-1/4}) with O(1) batch. Muon-VR1 (equivalent, after rescaling M_t, to the practical Muon update M_t = mu*C_t + grad f): also O(T^{-1/4}). Only VR2 reaches Otilde(T^{-1/3}).
locator: Table 1 (rows 'Ours / Option EMA' and 'Ours / Option VR1'); Theorems 4.1, 4.2, 4.4, 4.5
notes: Opposing evidence against treating the Nesterov/momentum-form detail of our Muon as a promising lever: theory says it buys no rate, and the paper's own LM curves put VR1 close to EMA. Transfer 2 -- these are worst-case upper bounds under assumptions (bounded variance, L-smoothness) that language modelling violates, so they cannot rule out a real empirical difference, but they argue the expected effect size is small relative to our noise floor. Useful for pruning, not for launching.
statement: The Nesterov-style one-batch momentum form of Muon used in practice has the same O(T^{-1/4}) worst-case convergence rate as plain EMA momentum Muon; only the two-batch variance-reduced form improves the rate.

comparator: 124M GPT-2 in the nanoGPT framework on OpenWebText, against SGD, AdamW, Shampoo and Muon. No per-optimizer tuning protocol, seed count, batch size or horizon is stated anywhere in the paper.
effect: Reported only as curve ordering: fastest loss reduction and lowest final loss over the entire trajectory, ahead of Muon, with the same ordering in train and validation. No numeric losses, no step count, no wall-clock.
locator: Section 6 Experimental Results, Figure 1(a) and 1(b)
notes: Internal validity 1: this is a figure with no numbers, no seeds, no tuning protocol and no reported step budget, in a paper whose substance is the theory. Transfer 2 despite being at exactly our 124M nanoGPT operating point, because the method computes P^{-1/2} and Q^{-1/2} inverse square roots of Kronecker factors every step via Gauss-Seidel updates plus a Newton-Schulz polar step, and the per-step cost of that is never reported -- decisive at 300 charged seconds where step count dominates. Worth at most one cheap throughput probe (measure step time first, before measuring loss).
statement: A Kronecker-factored Fisher-preconditioned orthogonalized-momentum optimizer reached lower training and validation loss than Muon, AdamW, Shampoo and SGD across the whole training horizon on a 124M-parameter GPT-2 trained with nanoGPT on OpenWebText.

comparator: Condition number of update matrices tracked over training for Adam, Muon at NS=5, Muon at NS=7 and FISMO; the optimality argument is imported from cited theory, not tested by an ablation in this paper.
effect: kappa_Adam > 1e8; kappa_FISMO in 1e2-1e3; kappa_Muon(NS=5) > kappa_Muon(NS=7) > kappa_ideal = 1. More Newton-Schulz iterations enforce stricter orthogonalization and push kappa toward 1; the argument (following the isotropic curvature model of Su 2025) is that under realistic super-quadratic curvature growth the optimal update compresses singular values without equalizing them, so a kappa bounded away from 1 may beat kappa = 1.
locator: Section 7 'A Condition Number Perspective', Figure 3
notes: Transfer 3 -- the highest here -- purely because the Newton-Schulz iteration count is a free scalar in our train.py that the paper shows directly moves kappa, and lowering it also SAVES FLOPs, so the throughput and hypothesis directions align for once. Registered as boundary, not supports, because the paper never runs an experiment varying NS count and measuring loss: the chain 'fewer NS iterations -> larger kappa -> better' is my reading of two separate statements, and the paper's own vehicle for larger kappa is a different (expensive) preconditioner. Internal validity 2: the kappa measurement itself is direct, the optimality claim is borrowed.
statement: The measured average condition number of update matrices orders as Adam (>1e8) >> Fisher-preconditioned (1e2-1e3) > practical Muon with 5 Newton-Schulz iterations > Muon with 7 iterations > 1, and the paper argues the optimal spectral transform is partial rather than strict spectrum homogenization.

comparator: Standard cosine (warmup then cosine decay, fixed exponent 1) with its own separately tuned base learning rate, same workload, same step budget; medians over seeds with DKW confidence intervals.
effect: WikiText-103 (8M-param transformer, 1600 steps, batch 512): median training perplexity 26.6-26.7 for the best flexible families vs 27.2 for cosine (about 2% relative). CIFAR-10 (1000 steps): median training error 0.063-0.064 (two-point spline, sqrt decay, generalized cosine, two-point linear) vs 0.092 for cosine.
locator: Section 4.2 'Flexible families provide small but significant gains'; Figure 5
notes: Transfer 4 and internal validity 4 -- the strongest claim in this batch. Protocol: ~600 shapes per family on WikiText-103, each at 16 base LRs, 5 seeds during search, then the top 50 re-trained with 100 seeds (10 inits x 10 data orders) and scored by median. The operating point matches ours closely: 1600 steps, AdamW, deliberately optimization-limited (so schedules are separable), and a decay-shape change costs zero throughput in train.py. Caveats stated by the authors: WikiText-103 standard errors are larger than CIFAR's because some near-optimal-schedule runs go unstable with very large perplexities, and the gains are 'small but significant' -- roughly 2%, which is well above our 5-minute-frame noise floor but is a training-loss (not held-out) metric at 8M params, not 124M.
statement: In an optimization-limited 1600-step small-transformer language modelling run, the best searched decay shapes reached lower median training perplexity than standard cosine decay, with the base learning rate separately tuned for every shape.

comparator: Across the eight schedule families, comparing the sensitivity of the score to base LR against sensitivity to shape parameters, at matched step budgets.
effect: Stated for all families except Constant, on both CIFAR-10 and WikiText-103; the authors also warn that a new schedule family must have its base LR re-tuned from scratch or the comparison produces false negatives. They further note that for non-linear models there is a non-trivial range of learning rates ABOVE the optimum that do not diverge.
locator: Section 4.2 'Base learning rate is the most important factor for a good schedule'; Figure 3; section 5.2 practical takeaways
notes: Registered as opposing evidence against schedule-shape interventions being a high-yield direction, from the same >1e6-run search that produced the shape gains above -- so the two claims must be read together: the shape gain is real but second-order to base LR. Transfer 4: directly actionable for how we allocate runs, and it carries a hard methodological warning for our A/B harness, namely that any schedule-family change we test at the incumbent base LR will look like a null. The 'range above the optimum that does not diverge' observation is also useful given how thin our LR sweeps are.
statement: Once a schedule has both warmup and monotonic decay, the base learning rate is a much more important factor than the schedule family, and extra tuning budget is better spent on the base learning rate than on schedule-shape hyperparameters.

comparator: Best members of each family, including the unconstrained 'snm' family, against each other and against the analytically optimal linear-regression schedule.
effect: Warmup fractions of 10-30% of total training on both CIFAR-10 and WikiText-103. Across a WikiText-103 training-horizon sweep, warmup FRACTION stayed consistent while longer horizons favored gentler decay. In contrast the optimal linear-regression schedule has no warmup at all and a flat-then-sharp-decay shape.
locator: Section 4.2 'Warmup and monotonic decay are both crucial'; section 4.4 'Varying the training horizon'; Figure 14
notes: Transfer 3: supports specifying warmup as a fraction of the run rather than a fixed step count, which matters concretely for us because our step count is set by throughput and moves whenever an intervention changes step time -- a fixed warmup step count silently changes the warmup fraction across arms and confounds A/Bs. 10-30% is a wide band and is measured at 8M params on 1600 steps, so treat the range as a prior, not a setting. The authors also flag that the unconstrained family was the one family their search did NOT explore adequately, which slightly weakens the 'rediscovery' half.
statement: The best schedules on both workloads used non-trivial warmup of 10-30% of total training, and an unconstrained spline family with neither warmup nor decay built in rediscovered warmup plus monotonic decay by random search.

comparator: The same searched schedule shapes re-run under each beta2 value, 100 seeds, median scoring; the comparator is the identical schedule at a different beta2.
effect: WikiText-103 median training perplexity when evaluating at beta2 = 0.9: 26.23, 26.32, 26.32, 26.36 across the four selection conditions, versus 26.59-26.87 at beta2 = 0.999 and 26.71-26.77 at 0.9995; the beta2 = 0.9 column also has by far the tightest reported spread (+-0.01 to 0.02 versus up to +-11.37 at 0.9995). CIFAR-10 Table 4 shows the same ordering.
locator: Section 4.4, Table 5 (WikiText-103) and Table 4 (CIFAR-10)
notes: Transfer 3: a one-line AdamW change with zero throughput cost, measured at 1600 steps on a transformer LM in the optimization-limited regime, which is close to our regime; a short second-moment timescale is mechanistically plausible when the whole run is 600-1000 steps. Internal validity 3, not 4: beta2 was not the pre-registered variable -- the authors read these tables as evidence that beta2 does NOT affect which schedule shapes are good, and give no CI on the roughly 0.4-perplexity (1.5%) gap. Note the paper's own text emphasizes the diagonal-vs-off-diagonal reading; the column-wise ordering I am extracting is consistent across all four rows but is my aggregation of their table.
statement: Running searched schedules at AdamW beta2 = 0.9 gave the lowest median training perplexity in every selection condition on the 1600-step WikiText-103 workload, beating beta2 = 0.999 and 0.9995, with the same direction on CIFAR-10.

comparator: Same searched schedules re-run at each beta1 value, 100 seeds, median scoring.
effect: Best median training perplexity 26.91 at beta1 = 0.95 (from schedules selected at 0.95 or 0.975), versus 30.47-30.51 at beta1 = 0.975, 26.92-28.2 at 0.9, and 28.8-40.61 at 0.8 where the spread is widest (+-0.96 to +-4.09).
locator: Section 4.4, Table 3
notes: Transfer 3: zero-cost knob, measured on a transformer LM at a step budget close to ours. The non-monotonicity is the useful part -- 0.975 is much worse than 0.95, so momentum is not a 'higher is better' knob at short horizons, which cuts against the theory-side prescription in 2603.15958 that momentum beta should be pushed toward 1 under a batch cap. Held at internal validity 3 because beta1 was varied to probe schedule-shape interaction, not as a clean optimizer ablation, and the 8M model has different gradient-noise structure than our 124M.
statement: On the 1600-step WikiText-103 workload, training perplexity was lowest when running at AdamW beta1 = 0.95 and clearly worse at both 0.975 and 0.8.

comparator: Same searched schedule shapes re-run at each weight decay value, 100 seeds, median scoring; comparator is the identical schedule at lambda_WD = 0.
effect: WikiText-103 median training perplexity at evaluation: 26.75-29.16 at lambda_WD = 0, 27.05-30.93 at 0.001, 69.48-165.99 at 0.01, and 392.74-5336.9 at 0.1. CIFAR-10 training error: 0.067-0.109 at 0, versus 0.406-0.532 at 0.01 and 0.839-0.9 at 0.1.
locator: Section 4.4 'Varying lambda_WD'; Table 7 (WikiText-103) and Table 6 (CIFAR-10)
notes: Transfer 2, deliberately not higher. The metric is TRAINING loss by design, and the authors say so ('as we would expect since we are comparing training metrics'), so this cannot separate 'weight decay hurts optimization' from 'weight decay helps generalization'. That partly favors us -- our objective is single-epoch val_bpb where train and val track closely and there is little overfitting to regularize -- but the magnitudes are implausible to import: an 8M model with a base-LR grid spanning 1e-4 to 1e-1 means the lambda*eta product at the top of the grid is enormous, and standard LLM pretraining runs at wd 0.1 without perplexity collapsing. Treat as: at our horizon, weight decay is a candidate to REDUCE, and the reduction should be swept jointly with LR, not as a free win.
statement: Zero or near-zero decoupled weight decay gave the best training metrics on both workloads, and larger weight decay was strongly harmful at these short horizons.

comparator: Optimal two-point-spline shapes found at each lambda_WD, cross-evaluated at every other lambda_WD, 100 seeds.
effect: Small weight-decay values lengthen the warmup; large values keep the rate high until the final training steps. Cross-evaluation shows schedules selected at a given lambda_WD are indeed best at that lambda_WD, confirming a real interaction rather than search noise. Weight decay was the ONLY hyperparameter among beta1, beta2 and lambda_WD to show a strong effect on optimal shape.
locator: Section 4.4 'Varying lambda_WD'; Figure 13; cross-evaluation Tables 6 and 7
notes: Transfer 2: it means weight decay and schedule shape are NOT separable knobs for us -- changing one invalidates the tuning of the other, which is a direct warning for our one-knob-at-a-time A/B protocol. Not scored higher because the effect is shown as schedule curves in a figure rather than quantified, and both workloads are far below our parameter scale. Practical use: if we lower weight decay per the previous claim, re-check the decay onset in the same experiment rather than in a later one.
statement: Increasing decoupled weight decay shifted the optimal learning-rate schedule toward decaying later, i.e. holding the rate high until near the end of training, on both workloads.

comparator: A fixed nuGPT model (depth = n_heads = 12) with the token-count correction removed, swept over iteration counts; comparator is the same model at other horizons. Adam with weight decay 0.0, beta1 = 0.9, beta2 = 0.95, eps = 1e-16, no warmup, cosine to 10% of peak, FineWeb-Edu, sequence length 4096, batch 64 (262144 tokens/step).
effect: Power-law fit of optimal peak LR vs iteration count with exponent about -1/3; matches Bjorck et al. (beta = 0.32) on un-normalized transformers and is said to be independently confirmed in a third setting.
locator: Section 4.6 'Token count correction' and Figure 9; section 3.3
notes: Transfer 2. The per-step token count (262144) is within 2x of ours and the data is FineWeb-Edu, which is close to our shard set, so the setup is unusually comparable in those respects. But the sweep is at >=0.26B parameters and horizons around 80000 steps, and using a fit made over tens of thousands of steps to predict how peak LR should move between, say, 700 and 850 steps is a long extrapolation into the burn-in regime. Figure-only result, no table, and the paper's seed averaging (3 seeds) is stated for other figures, not clearly for this one.
statement: In a fixed-size normalized-transformer model swept over iteration counts, the optimal peak learning rate decreased as roughly (iteration count)^{-1/3}, matching an independently reported exponent of 0.32 for un-normalized transformers.

comparator: Their own iteration-count sweep and fits, against the published -1/2 theoretical prescription.
effect: States that the SDE-derived and separately theory-derived m_data^{-1/2} correction (attributed to Mlodozeniec et al. 2025 and Shulgin et al. 2026) has an exponent that is 'too large', and substitutes m_data^{-1/3}.
locator: Section 3.3 'Token horizon corrections'
notes: Registered as opposing evidence because 'Shulgin et al. 2026' is 2603.15958 in this same batch, whose Regime (A) transfer rule is exactly eta_1 = eta_0 (T_0/T_1)^{1/2}. The two papers directly disagree about the exponent, and the disagreement is between a bound-minimization proxy and an empirical fit, so the empirical fit should be weighted higher for our purposes. Transfer 2 because both exponents are calibrated far outside our horizon; the practical takeaway is that the horizon correction is real and downward but its magnitude is uncertain by at least a factor 1.5 in the exponent, which is large enough that we should measure it on our own frame rather than import either rule.
statement: The authors explicitly reject the theoretically predicted token-horizon learning-rate exponent of -1/2 as too large, choosing -1/3 on the basis of their own and others' power-law fits.

comparator: None run in this paper: the no-warmup / no-weight-decay property is inherited from Loshchilov et al. 2025 and adopted as a setup choice, not ablated here. This paper's own contribution is that BASELINE nGPT fails to transfer learning rate across width and token horizon (Figures 1a, 2a).
effect: All of the paper's runs use AdamW with weight decay 0.0, no warm-up, cosine decay to 10% of peak, eps = 1e-16. The authors note the absence of weight decay is itself convenient because weight decay is 'a confounder for HP transfer theory'.
locator: Section 1 Introduction; section 4 Experiments (training setup); section 5 concluding remarks
notes: Transfer 2. Eliminating warmup is attractive for us in principle -- the previous claim set says warmup takes 10-30% of the run, and steps spent below peak LR are expensive at 600-1000 total steps -- but this paper provides no evidence that removing warmup alone helps; the property is a package deal with full weight normalization, which is an architecture change with a per-step renormalization cost charged against our step count. Held at internal validity 2 because nothing here is ablated. The paper's actual finding, that baseline nGPT does not transfer LR, is irrelevant to us (fixed model size) but is a signal the configuration is delicate.
statement: The Normalized Transformer, which constrains weight and activation norms by normalizing every weight matrix and adds trainable scale parameters, is trained without weight decay and without learning-rate warmup while reporting training speedups.

comparator: Muon and Muon-Nesterov (Moonlight impl, 2D weights on Muon, 1D+embeddings on AdamW), identical architecture/data/recipe, LR tuned per optimizer on pilot runs; 64 Ascend 910C NPUs.
effect: LLaMA2-130M / 10.5B tokens: val ppl 19.56 for MuonEq-R vs 20.52 for Muon and 20.18 for Muon-Nesterov (-0.47 vs the better Muon baseline); at 350M / 21B tokens 14.96 vs 15.21 / 15.19.
locator: section 4.1, table 1
notes: Transfer 3: param count (130M) and tokens/step (128 x 4096 = 524288) match our operating point almost exactly, and the change is ~10 lines inside the Muon step (rowsum of M*M, rsqrt, scale). Discount is horizon: 10.5B tokens = ~20000 steps vs our 600-1000, and MuonEq's own diagnostics (fig 7) show the geometry gap is largest EARLY, so the sign is plausible but the magnitude at 600 steps is untested. Single run per cell, no seeds, no error bars.
statement: Row-normalizing the momentum matrix before Newton-Schulz orthogonalization (MuonEq-R) lowers best validation perplexity versus plain Muon at 130M params on C4.

comparator: Muon-Nesterov with identical NS budget, optimizer state, scalar hyperparameters and LR grid {5e-4,1e-3,2e-3,5e-3}; only the diagonal map before NS changes. 4x RTX Pro6000.
effect: FineWeb 10.5B tokens, GPT2-small, 20000 steps: MuonEq-R 24.94, MuonEq-RC 24.98, MuonEq-C 25.23, Muon-Nesterov 25.31, AdamW 26.60 validation perplexity.
locator: section 4.2, table 3 (and appendix J.2)
notes: Transfer 3: GPT2-small on FineWeb is our closest sibling workload and only the optimizer changes, so it is directly portable. But the R-vs-RC gap (0.04 ppl) is far below anything we could resolve at n=1 in a 5-minute frame; only the ~0.37 ppl gap to Muon-Nesterov is a candidate effect. 20000 steps vs our ~600-1000 is the main discount. No seeds reported.
statement: Among pre-orthogonalization equilibration variants on GPT2-small/FineWeb, row (R) and two-sided row/col (RC) are near-identical and both beat column-only (C) and plain Muon-Nesterov.

comparator: Muon / Muon-Nesterov on the same 64-NPU setup; AdamW is 0.21 s/step at 130M.
effect: 130M: 0.26 s/step for MuonEq vs 0.25 for Muon (+4%); 350M: 0.63 vs 0.61 (+3%); peak memory identical (12.52 GB / 28.18 GB) because auxiliary state is only O(m+n).
locator: section 4.1, table 1 (Time Cost / Memory columns)
notes: Transfer 3: the cost is a real, measured, small number and the memory claim is structural (O(m+n)). At our operating point the accounting is even more favourable, since ~94% of charged time is the CPU packing loop and a couple of extra element-wise reductions on GPU are close to free; but on their NPUs a 4% step-time hit would cost ~4% of our step budget, so it must be measured, not assumed.
statement: Pre-orthogonalization row/column equilibration costs about 4% per-step wall clock and no additional peak memory over Muon.

comparator: Direct (no preconditioning), ColNorm, RowNorm on the same trajectory; diagnostic norms, not loss.
effect: Layerwise ||NS5(S(M)) - Orth(S(M))||_F is lowest or near-lowest for RowColNorm at steps 1% and 10% of a 2.6B-token LLaMA2-130M run; by 50-100% the top-panel differences 'shrink substantially' while RC's bias term stays largest. RowColNorm also gives consistently higher singular-value entropy and stable rank than Direct/Row/Col.
locator: appendix I, figures 6 and 7 (module-wise pre-NS momentum analysis)
notes: Transfer 2 and stance boundary because this is a diagnostic (spectral) measurement, not a loss measurement, and the paper still defaults to R on a loss basis. It matters to us because OUR ENTIRE RUN lives in their 1-10%-of-training window, which is exactly where they say the two-sided variant does the most spectral work - so the paper's own default (R) may be the wrong choice at a 600-step horizon and RC deserves the A/B. Read as a hypothesis generator, not evidence of a loss win.
statement: Two-sided RC equilibration reduces the finite-step Newton-Schulz approximation error most at 1-10% of training and the advantage largely disappears by 50-100%, at the price of the largest preconditioning bias throughout.

comparator: Warmup+cosine annealing on the same models; no final-loss numbers or seeds are reported for the schedule comparison.
effect: Qualitative only: identical curve shape for a 160M Pythia-style LM (3B tokens, batch 256 x 2048) and a 334K-param CNN on CIFAR-10 (50 epochs); sharpness (top Hessian eigenvalue) increases along the decay iterates, and the PCA direction of early cooldown has larger ||H v|| than the stable-phase direction in both models.
locator: section 3 (Figures 1-3): River Valley, Sharpness, Cooldown unveils a sharp tunnel
notes: Transfer 2: mechanism-level support that the decay phase is where measured loss is realised, which matters for us because a 600-1000 step run spends a large fraction of its life in one phase or the other and the split point is a free knob. Scored no higher because the paper reports zero final-loss numbers, no seed counts, and makes no claim about optimal cooldown fraction. Internal validity 2: descriptive/diagnostic study, small n, figures only.
statement: Under WSD the loss decreases only modestly during the stable phase and drops sharply during cooldown, and this pattern plus its landscape signature is not specific to transformers.

comparator: None; the paper runs no experiments of its own.
effect: No numbers - this is a narrative survey with only qualitative tables (tables 1-4). The assertion is that a method can reduce loss faster initially and converge to a worse final loss, and vice versa, especially when methods differ in implicit regularization or update geometry.
locator: section 11.6 'Early-Training Curves and Final Performance' and section 11.13 'Early-curve overclaiming'
notes: Internal validity 1 because it is a secondary source with zero first-party evidence: I checked every table and found no perplexity or loss number in the whole document. Transfer 2 only because it is the campaign's own transfer policy stated from the other side - our objective IS the early curve, so published long-horizon optimizer wins are not evidence for us and should be re-measured in-frame. Do not treat this as support for or against any specific intervention.
statement: Optimizer rankings taken from early training curves do not reliably predict rankings at the end of a full token budget.

comparator: The matched decoupled-weight-decay version of each optimizer on the public Track 3 logs (model, data and tokens fixed; the benchmark metric is step count to a loss band).
effect: AdamH reaches average val loss 3.2741 in 4875 steps vs AdamW 3.2790 in 5625 steps; MuonH 3.2782 vs MuonW 3.2790, both in 3325 steps; NorMuonH 3.2778 vs NorMuonW 3.2789 at 3250 steps; KL-SOAP-H 3.2780 in 3125 steps.
locator: section 3.2, figure 4 (modded-nanogpt Track 3 comparison)
notes: Transfer 4: this is the only evidence in the batch measured on a ~124M-class GPT with fixed data at 3000-5600 steps, i.e. within a factor of ~5 of our horizon, and the wrapper is a few lines (normalize u, step by eta*R, renormalize W to R; embeddings/gains stay on Adam). Caveats to carry: the Muon-side margin is 0.0008 loss, far inside our noise band, so only the Adam-side step saving (-13%) is a resolvable-size effect; numbers come from public leaderboard logs rather than the authors' own controlled seeds; and Track 3's fixed model may not have our VE/SSSL structure.
statement: Wrapping the base optimizer so weight and update Frobenius norms are held constant (Hyperball) reaches a target validation loss in fewer steps than the matched weight-decay baseline on the modded-nanogpt Track 3 benchmark.

comparator: MuonW / AdamW with decoupled weight decay under the same LR schedule.
effect: Qualitative crossover: at 1.2B the MuonH advantage 'grows with training duration' (10% for MuonW alone vs 20-30% for MuonH at 1x-8x Chinchilla), i.e. the gain is back-loaded and negative at the start.
locator: section 3.2 ('Qualitatively, Hyperball starts slightly worse but overtakes WD as the learning rate decays'), figure 2
notes: Transfer 3 and registered as OPPOSING because our whole run is the pre-crossover region: at ~600-1000 steps and ~4 tokens/param we live in the early regime where the paper says Hyperball is behind. This is the single most important caveat on the claim above and the two must be carried together - the Track 3 result shows the crossover can happen inside a few-thousand-step run, but not that it happens inside 600.
statement: Hyperball is slightly WORSE than the weight-decay baseline early in training and only overtakes it as the learning rate decays.

comparator: A scaling law fit to AdamW across Chinchilla ratios {1,2,4,8}x; speedup tau = N_AdamW/N_method at matched final loss.
effect: 20-30% token-equivalent speedup for MuonH vs ~10% for MuonW, at 1.2B params over Chinchilla ratios 1x-8x; overtrained 130M sweep fits L_inf = 3.065 (MuonH) vs 3.079 (MuonW) over 1B-128B token budgets.
locator: section 3.2, figure 2; abstract
notes: Transfer 1: 1.2B params at 1x-8x Chinchilla (>=24B tokens) is 10x our params and >30x our token budget, and the 130M overtrained sweep starts at 1B tokens (~2x our whole budget) and is fit through the asymptote. The mechanism is the same as the Track 3 claim, so this adds scale-robustness rather than in-regime evidence. Do not use it to justify a run on its own.
statement: At 1.2B params Hyperball sustains a 20-30% token-equivalent speedup over the AdamW scaling law where plain Muon with weight decay gives only about 10%.

comparator: Each other (paired ablation, everything else fixed).
effect: Two 1.2B AdamW runs with (eta, lambda) = (0.002, 0.2) and (0.004, 0.1), same product 4e-4: train loss curves nearly overlap while layer-9 Q/K weight norms roughly double in the larger-LR run.
locator: section 4.3, Phenomenon 3, figure 10
notes: Transfer 2: if it holds here it collapses a 2D (lr, wd) search to 1D, which is worth a lot at n=1. The reason it is not 3: the invariance is an EQUILIBRIUM property - it requires the radial dynamics to have converged to the weight-decay fixed point, and at 600-1000 steps with eta*lambda ~ 1e-4 per step the weights have barely moved off initialization, so the equilibrium may never be reached in our frame. Test the invariance directly before relying on it. n=2 runs, 1.2B, no seeds.
statement: For scale-invariant matrix weights, holding the product of learning rate and weight decay fixed leaves the training loss essentially unchanged while the equilibrium weight norm scales proportionally to the learning rate.

comparator: The same model and LR schedule with weight decay turned off.
effect: Qualitative crossover in a paired WD vs no-WD comparison: without WD the weight norm grows and the angular step proxy eta*||u||_F/||W||_F decays; with WD the effective step stays larger, which raises early loss (more 'hill' oscillation) but yields lower loss after the decay phase.
locator: section 4.3, Phenomenon 4, figure 11
notes: Transfer 3 and registered as OPPOSING: this says weight decay is a net loss-increaser over most of a run and only pays off through the decay phase. At 600-1000 steps we should not assume the standard nonzero weight decay is helping - it is a cheap A/B (wd=0 vs wd=0.1) and the paper predicts the sign could go either way depending on how much of our run is cooldown. Mechanistic account is explicit (effective/angular step size), evidence is one paired figure at 1.2B without seeds.
statement: Under an identical learning-rate schedule, a run with weight decay has HIGHER loss early in training and only crosses below the no-weight-decay run once the learning rate decays.

comparator: Muon and Cautious-Muon with identical LR, schedule and step budget; bf16, cosine-to-10% with 10% warmup.
effect: ~1.2x speedup over Muon on LLaMA2-71M (hidden 512, depth 12, 2034 steps, batch 480 x 1024, lr 3e-4) and 1.1x on Qwen2.5-150M (1525 steps, batch 160 x 1024, lr 1e-3), with tau=gamma=1/alpha=0.5.
locator: section 5.1, figures 3a and 4 (LLaMA2-71M and Qwen2.5-150M on WikiText-103)
notes: Transfer 3: the step counts (1525-2034) and model sizes (71M/150M, hidden 512) are the closest match in this batch, and the change is a topk on |u*g| plus two scalar multipliers inside the optimizer. Two discounts: (a) 'speedup' is read off validation curves with no stated protocol, no seeds and no final-loss table, so internal validity is 2; (b) WikiText-103 is only ~103M tokens, so these runs are 2-10 EPOCHS - a memorization regime that our own campaign has already shown inverts lever signs versus a single-epoch fresh-shard run.
statement: Amplifying the step size on the top-K coordinates by momentum-gradient alignment and damping the rest (MGUP) gives a modest speedup over plain Muon in short small-model pretraining runs.

comparator: Standard AdamW / Lion / Muon and their Cautious variants at the same LR (3e-4) and schedule.
effect: 1.6x speedup for MGUP-AdamW over AdamW and 2.5x for MGUP-Lion over Lion on LLaMA2-71M / WikiText-103 / 2034 steps, versus ~1.2x for MGUP-Muon.
locator: section 5.1, figure 3a
notes: Transfer 3 for implementability and scale, but note the direct implication for a Muon+AdamW hybrid like ours: the benefit is concentrated on the ADAMW-side parameter group (embeddings, gains, 1D params), which is the smaller share of our update. Same caveats as the Muon claim: curve-read speedups, no seeds, multi-epoch WikiText-103.
statement: The same top-K alignment rule gives a larger speedup on AdamW and Lion than on Muon at 71M scale.

comparator: AdamW and Cautious-AdamW on the same single RTX 4090 (7B case on 2x V100).
effect: LLaMA2-71M WikiText-103 pretraining 5h36m (AdamW) -> 5h37m (MGUP-AdamW), +0.3%; Qwen2.5-150M 1h54m -> 1h56m, +1.8%; ViT-28M 1h5m -> 1h6m. Fine-tuning overhead is much larger (RoBERTa QQP 25m -> 34m, +36%). Peak reserved memory 32.09 GB -> 33.82 GB at 7B fine-tuning.
locator: appendix I.1 table 8 and I.2 table 9
notes: Transfer 3: the pretraining overhead numbers are directly the quantity we care about, and they say a global sort over the parameter vector is nearly free at 71M-150M scale when the batch is large. Two hazards: their own remark I.1 says these are end-to-end durations on a possibly-shared GPU, so +/-2% is within their measurement noise; and the fine-tuning rows (micro-batch 1) show the sort DOES dominate when the per-step compute is small - our step is large, so we should be on the favourable side, but it must be measured.
statement: The top-K alignment wrapper adds under 2% wall clock in small-model pretraining, though it raises transient peak memory.

comparator: AdamW / Lion / Muon without the cautious mask, same LR and schedule.
effect: C-AdamW 'gradually falls behind' AdamW on ViT-MAE/CIFAR-10 training and validation loss; C-Lion shows early loss spikes and instability on LLaMA2-71M; on GLUE C-AdamW averages 83.69 vs AdamW 84.74.
locator: section 5.1, figure 2 (ViT-MAE) and figure 3a; table 1 (GLUE)
notes: Transfer 2: registered as opposing evidence for the cautious-masking family, which is otherwise a tempting cheap lever. Discounts: the LM evidence is a curve read at 71M with no seeds, the strongest numeric evidence (GLUE) is fine-tuning and therefore out of our regime, and the ViT-MAE result is a vision task. Enough to de-prioritise a plain cautious mask, not enough to rule it out.
statement: Cautious optimizers (hard-masking updates whose sign disagrees with the gradient) underperform their plain counterparts in this study.

comparator: Grid over tau x gamma on LLaMA2-71M / WikiText-103 / 2034 steps, all other hyperparameters fixed.
effect: With tau fixed, larger gamma generally improved validation loss (gamma=0, i.e. fully zeroing misaligned coordinates, was worst); with gamma fixed, increasing tau beyond a threshold degraded performance. Recommended default tau=gamma=0.5, which also maximises the average step inflation factor (1 + tau - tau^2).
locator: section 5.1, figure 3b (sensitivity over tau in {0.3,0.5,0.7} and gamma in {0,0.1,0.5,0.9}); appendix A counterexample
notes: Transfer 3: this is the operational detail that decides whether a cheap alignment-gating experiment succeeds or fails, and it directly explains the cautious-optimizer result above (cautious = gamma 0). Also note the paper's own mechanism: the gain may be nothing more than a (1 + tau - tau^2) = 1.25x inflation of the average step size, i.e. an LR retune in disguise - so any A/B must include an LR-matched control or it proves nothing. Curve-read grid, no seeds.
statement: Setting the damping factor for non-selected coordinates to zero degrades performance; a nonzero damping factor and a selection fraction near one half work best.

comparator: Per-horizon separately tuned cosine baselines (the 'cosine envelope'), same OLMo 150M model on C4, AdamW, no weight decay, no data repetition.
effect: 150M model at batch size 4096 (x1024 seq len): constant LR + averaging 'substantially outperforms cosine for all horizons beyond 1x Chinchilla', and the LR that is near-optimal for long runs stays near-optimal throughout; 1/sqrt(t) with averaging also improves over cosine but underperforms constant. Magnitudes are figure-only (no table).
locator: section 3.2, figure 3 (and appendix B.2 figure 6)
notes: Transfer 2: mechanism (large batch suppresses gradient noise so decay is not needed to control variance) plausibly applies to us since 524288 tokens/step at a 0.5B-token budget is well above any sensible CBS, and EMA is a cheap one-extra-parameter-copy add-on evaluated only at the end. Held at 2 because every measured horizon is >= 1x Chinchilla (>= 3.3B tokens, ~6300 steps at our step size) and the effect is reported only as figures with no numbers or seeds. Note this claim CONFLICTS with 2605.19095's finding that linear decay beats constant-type schedules; the discriminator is batch size relative to CBS.
statement: Far above the critical batch size, a constant learning rate with EMA weight averaging beats a tuned cosine schedule at every horizon tested.

comparator: Per-horizon tuned cosine baselines trained as separate runs; the anytime methods come from one long run evaluated at intermediate checkpoints.
effect: Across 1x-32x Chinchilla for 150M (batch 256) and 1x-16x for 300M (batch 512), constant+averaging and 1/sqrt(t)+averaging 'closely match cosine annealing, paying only a negligible performance hit near the start and end of training'.
locator: section 1.1 and section 3.1, figure 2 (right panels: loss difference vs cosine)
notes: Transfer 2, registered as OPPOSING: their shortest measured horizon (1x Chinchilla) is already ~6x our token budget, and that is precisely where they report the anytime schedules are BEHIND cosine. Read together with the large-batch claim, the honest reading for us is: replacing our decay schedule with constant+EMA is a coin flip that depends on where our batch sits relative to CBS, and the short-horizon evidence leans against it. Figures only, no seeds.
statement: At the critical batch size, horizon-free schedules with averaging only match a tuned cosine schedule, and are slightly worse near the very start of training.

comparator: The optimal cosine envelope: an independently tuned cosine decay for each terminal budget, best validation loss at that budget.
effect: Intermediate checkpoints of cosine runs tuned for 8x/16x/32x Chinchilla lie 'substantially below' (i.e. worse than) the per-horizon optimal cosine envelope, at both 150M and 300M. Gap is shown graphically only.
locator: section 1 figure 1 and appendix B.4 figure 10
notes: Transfer 3: this is a discipline claim that applies at any scale and is free to act on - our LR schedule (peak, warmup fraction, decay shape) must be re-tuned for a 600-1000 step run and never inherited from a longer-horizon recipe or from published defaults. It also warns that comparing two interventions at different step counts under one fixed schedule is confounded, which matters for any throughput-changing lever we test.
statement: A cosine schedule tuned for a long horizon is substantially worse at shorter budgets than a cosine tuned to that budget.

comparator: Last-iterate evaluation (f=0) of the same runs; cosine decay as the practical baseline.
effect: Theory: for overparameterized linear regression, eta_t = 1/t^gamma with tail averaging attains the minimax SGD rate for 0<gamma<1; without averaging polynomially decaying schedules generally do NOT. Empirically all reported anytime runs use an EMA with half-life a fixed fraction of t, sweeping f in {6.25, 12.5, 25, 50, 100} (f=0 is last-iterate, no averaging).
locator: section 1.1 (theorem, informal) and section 3 'Averaging'; theoretical analysis section 4
notes: Transfer 2: the actionable version for us is that maintaining one EMA of the weights and evaluating val_bpb from the EMA copy is a ~free measurement-side intervention (one extra fp32 copy, one axpy per step, no change to the training trajectory) that could pay off without costing steps. Held at 2 because the theory is linear regression and the LM evidence is all at >= 1x Chinchilla; the half-life fraction would need retuning at 600 steps where 'the last 1/f of iterates' is a very small window.
statement: Weight averaging, not the step-size shape, is the component that lets horizon-free learning rates reach the performance of a decayed schedule.

comparator: Tuned linear-decay and WSD schedules with AdamW at matched token budgets, 120M-2B params, FineWeb-EDU-style data, LR grid-searched for the baselines.
effect: 'No final loss advantage is seen for short duration (20-100 TPP) runs.' At 20 TPP (120M model, 2289 steps, 1M-token batches) ScheduleFree+ beats WSD at all scales but shows a gap versus linear decay at larger models; the paper states that at this TPP scale 'the duration of the run for which gradient norms and weight norms are not at steady state is close to 50% of the run' and that Schedule-Free takes longer to reach steady state. Beta-annealing is ineffective at 100 TPP and r=1 weighting only helps beyond ~30B tokens.
locator: abstract; section 9.2 'Shorter Duration Training Runs', tables 2 and 3
notes: Transfer 3 and OPPOSING: our run is ~4 tokens/param, five times shorter than the shortest regime where the author already reports the method loses its edge, and the stated cause (a burn-in fraction of the run before norms stabilise) gets strictly worse as the horizon shrinks - at 600 steps essentially the entire run is burn-in. This is a well-instrumented negative for schedule-free/averaging-instead-of-decay at our operating point and should block that direction absent in-frame evidence.
statement: Schedule-Free training shows no final-loss advantage at short token budgets, and part of the deficit is attributed to the fraction of the run spent before weight and gradient norms reach steady state.

comparator: WSD (warmup, constant, linear anneal over final 10%) and cosine with several min/max ratios, each with its own LR grid search, at matched horizons.
effect: 'The WSD schedule's practical performance is good, but it is consistently outperformed by the linear decay schedule in our experiments when tuned to the same training horizon.' Figure 14 (500M model at 20 and 100 tokens per parameter, both LR grid-searched): cosine ties or under-performs linear decay, and a cosine with a 0.1 min/max ratio is suboptimal versus smaller final ratios; differences among the other ratios are tiny.
locator: section 10 (final paragraph) and section 11, figure 14
notes: Transfer 3: the closest measured setting (500M at 20 TPP) is the shortest-horizon comparison in the paper and the intervention is a one-line schedule change with zero throughput cost - the cheapest candidate in this whole batch. Two cautions: linear decay is horizon-dependent, so it must be tuned to our exact step count (see 2602.03702); and the theoretical backing (worst-case-optimal schedule for nonsmooth convex problems with flat gradient norms) assumes flat gradient norms, which do not hold during our burn-in.
statement: A linear decay-to-zero schedule tuned to the training horizon consistently outperforms WSD, and cosine ties or underperforms linear decay.

comparator: Linear (b) LR scaling on the same sweep; batch sizes swept around 0.5M-4M tokens.
effect: On a 120M Llama-3-style model trained on FineWeb-EDU for 8B tokens, LR tuned at batch 1M tokens and transferred by sqrt(b): 'we confirmed experimentally that it outperforms linear scaling on this problem'. AdamW hits a scaling cliff at 4M tokens/batch; vanilla Schedule-Free cliffs earlier at 2M and needs inner momentum (beta1 = 0.75-0.9) to match.
locator: section 3 'Handling Larger Batch-Sizes', figure 2
notes: Transfer 3: 120M params on FineWeb-EDU is our model class and dataset class, and this is exactly the rule we need whenever a lever changes the effective batch or when we import an LR from a differently-batched reference. Discount: 8B tokens (~2000-8000 steps) is still 5-10x our horizon, and the claim is stated as a confirmed observation without a table.
statement: Scaling the learning rate with the square root of batch size outperforms linear scaling for AdamW-family optimizers at 120M scale.

comparator: Standard decoupled AdamW at the same weight decay and schedule.
effect: AdamW with a linear-decay schedule shows ~25% gradient-norm change after warmup while AdamC has 'nearly constant' gradient norm; AdamC 'slightly outperforms AdamW here' (120M, 8B tokens, WD 0.05), with a much larger gap for Schedule-Free. Mechanism: the steady state ||g||/||w|| = sqrt(2 lambda / gamma_max) becomes independent of the instantaneous LR.
locator: section 4, figure 4(a) and figure 5(a); section 6.1 equations 13-14
notes: Transfer 2: a two-character change in the optimizer (scale wd by gamma_t/gamma_max) with zero throughput cost, but the reported LM gain is 'slight' and unquantified, and the correction only bites where the LR varies a lot - in a 600-step run with a short decay the divergence between gamma_t and gamma_max is small and weight decay has barely acted at all. Worth bundling with a wd=0 control rather than testing alone.
statement: Multiplying the decoupled weight-decay term by an extra factor of the current-over-max learning rate (AdamC) flattens the gradient-norm trajectory and slightly improves loss over AdamW.

comparator: Constant (no-warmup) learning rate under the same assumptions; the synthetic river-valley example is tuned per schedule for the fastest non-diverging constant multiplier.
effect: Estimated smoothness L_hat(w_t) (max finite-difference gradient ratio over 6 interpolation points) shows a clear polynomial dependence on f(w)-f* for both a ResNet18/CIFAR-10 run and a NanoGPT (6 blocks, d=384, 6 heads) trained 600 steps on TinyShakespeare; theory then gives eta_t proportional to min(1/K0, Delta_t^{-rho}/(3^rho K_rho)), a monotonically increasing (i.e. warmup-shaped) schedule that provably beats a constant LR whenever K_rho > 0, by up to Theta(Delta_0 T) in a river-valley-like example.
locator: section 3.3 'Empirical Validation of the Assumption' (NanoGPT and ResNet18 log-log plots); section 4.1 theorems 1-2
notes: Transfer 2: the smoothness diagnostic is validated on a transformer at 600 steps - exactly our horizon - and the practical reading is concrete: warmup length should be set by how fast the loss gap drops, not by a fixed fraction, and its value grows with how bad the initial loss is. Held at 2 because there is no LM loss comparison anywhere in the paper; the schedule is only validated end-to-end on ResNet/CIFAR and a 2D synthetic. Implementing the adaptive schedule needs an estimate of f*, which is an extra hyperparameter (K0, K_rho were grid-searched).
statement: Local smoothness of the training loss is empirically a power law in the loss suboptimality gap, and is extremely large at initialization, which bounds the usable learning rate early and relaxes that bound as loss falls.

comparator: Constant schedule set to the SAME target learning rate as the warmup schedules (first 10 epochs warmup, cosine decay after), so the comparison deliberately removes the 'warmup lets you use a bigger peak LR' benefit.
effect: ResNet18/CIFAR-10, 100 epochs, SGD without momentum, 6 independent runs: theoretical warmup 0.8589 +/- 0.0023, linear warmup 0.8577 +/- 0.0023, no warmup (constant) 0.8562 +/- 0.0019 test accuracy. The warmup-vs-constant gap (0.0027) is only slightly larger than one standard deviation.
locator: section 4.2 'ResNet on CIFAR', table 1
notes: Transfer 1: vision task, SGD without momentum, 100 epochs - out of regime on every axis, and this is the only place in the paper where a warmup schedule is measured end to end. Registered as OPPOSING to keep the record honest: the paper's headline is a Theta(T) theoretical acceleration, but its own experiment shows a ~0.3pp effect at 6 seeds when the peak LR is held equal. Useful mainly as a warning that warmup-shape tinkering at fixed peak LR is a sub-noise lever; the peak LR itself is the real knob.
statement: The measured end-to-end gain from warmup over a constant learning rate, at matched target learning rate, is small and close to seed noise in the only end-to-end experiment reported.

comparator: Llama2-style transformer of matched size on DCLM, same training recipe (appendix E.2).
effect: 160M / 19B tokens / ctx 4096: Llama 21.03 vs mLSTM 20.89 (12 heads, exp gate, limit_chunk) to 21.18 (6 heads, xl_chunk). 400M / 24B: Llama 16.66 vs 16.55 best. 1.4B / 33B: Llama 13.31 vs 13.20 best. Some head-dim configurations show gradient-norm or loss spikes under the xl_chunk kernel that degrade final loss (e.g. 13.87 vs 13.20).
locator: section 5.1, table 2 (validation perplexity at context length 4096)
notes: Transfer 1: replacing softmax/sliding-window attention with a gated linear RNN is a whole-architecture swap requiring their Triton kernels, and the evidence is at 19B tokens (~36000 steps at our step size) where quality parity says nothing about the first 600 steps. The paper's own instability note (kernel-dependent loss spikes at some head dims) is a real risk at n=1. Recorded so the direction is not re-proposed without noticing the cost.
statement: An mLSTM linear-RNN sequence mixer matches a Llama2-style transformer on validation perplexity at 160M params and beats it at 400M and 1.4B.

comparator: FlashAttention-2/3 with 32 heads x head dim 128, Mamba2 and GLA kernels at matched token count.
effect: At 65,536 tokens held constant and embedding dim 4096 on H100: TFLA xl_chunk is faster than FlashAttention-3 for longer sequence lengths only, ~25% faster than the authors' own chunk-size-limited kernel, and the sigmoid input-gate variant adds >30% on the forward pass; Simple GLA is 3ms/15% faster still but at nearly 2x the GPU memory.
locator: section 5.2, figure 4 and appendix E.3
notes: Transfer 1 and OPPOSING for us: our attention is a SHORT sliding window (order 2^9-2^10) on a 124M model, i.e. exactly the short-sequence regime where the paper concedes FlashAttention-3 is still ahead, and our own profiling already shows attention is not the bottleneck (small n-gram GEMMs and tiny fill kernels are). Benchmarked at 7B-model width (4096), which further inflates linear attention's advantage relative to our d=512.
statement: Tiled linear-attention kernels beat FlashAttention-3 in forward+backward runtime only at longer sequence lengths, not across the board.

comparator: Deep vs wide Pre-LN at equal parameter count, each with its own tuned peak LR (3.0e-3 wide, 6.0e-3 deep).
effect: Fixed 3B params, 250B tokens, batch 1024 x 4096: the wide Pre-LN model (128 layers, hidden 2048) achieves lower training loss than the deep Pre-LN model (512 layers, hidden 1024), while average downstream scores are 52.2 vs 52.3.

The mechanism structurally requires (a) a truncated SVD of each gradient block per step (r_top = 2-8) and (b) an extra scalar evaluation of the global loss energy E^k per step - both hostile to our torch.compile'd single-pass 300s budget, and (b) is not even well-defined for a streaming minibatch objective. The one number worth carrying is the cost ordering: on small models orthogonalization overhead alone was ~1.8x Adam's wall clock, and the spectral extras added another 27%.
statement: The spectral-auxiliary-variable modification of Muon is evaluated only on deterministic scientific-ML objectives (linear regression, PINNs, DeepONet, fractional PINN-DeepONet) and increases wall-clock time over Muon, which itself was already far slower than Adam on those small models.

Implementable in train.py (it is an edit to the Muon update using two extra NS calls) but it introduces 3 new hyperparameters (chi, beta1, beta2, plus sharp-rank ratio r_s) which the authors grid-searched at 0.25B; we cannot afford that search at n=1 noise. Also note the baseline NS here is Polar Express with 6 iterations, not the ns_steps=5 vanilla NS we run, so the baseline is not our baseline.
statement: Selectively amplifying the Muon update along the estimated flat (non-top-singular) subspace, by a learning-rate ratio chi>1 plus a Hessian-damping gradient-correction term beta2, lowers terminal training loss versus a well-tuned vanilla Muon baseline across LLaMA 0.13B-1.3B on C4/Pile.

This is the single most decision-relevant result in the paper for us since the selective version needs a subspace projector we would have to build. Transfer 3: 0.25B is near our scale and the change is a one-line edit, but it is a 10k-iteration run at 1M-token batches (10x our steps) and only two beta values with no seeds, so the sign is more trustworthy than the magnitude. Directly relevant to the campaign's open contradiction on whether Nesterov-style momentum helps Muon.

comparator: WSD schedules with cooldown fraction swept over {0,0.05,...,0.95}, peak rate tuned separately at every point, 512 runs per point on quadratics / 8 on the deep linear net

locator: section 4 Prop. 2 and Lemma 1; section 5 Table 1; section 10 'Dissociation across models' and Table 3
notes: Transfer 2 and no higher: the evidence is quadratics, an (L0,L1) quartic, a deep linear net, and a 2-layer MLP on sklearn digits -- there is no transformer and no LM loss anywhere in this paper. It is registered because Muon's orthogonalized update is exactly the Theta(1)-magnitude class the theorem indicts, so the criterion predicts that decaying LR to (near) zero matters more for our Muon parameter group than for the AdamW group. Blocker for using it: the criterion is stated for stationary noise, and the authors explicitly say the mechanism cannot produce the interior cooldown fractions that actually work in pretraining.
statement: Optimizers whose update magnitude does not shrink as the gradient shrinks (sign-based and normalized methods) sit on a last-iterate loss floor of order eta^2 that only decaying the learning rate removes, while SGD-type updates self-anneal under gradient-proportional noise and prefer a constant rate.

comparator: 2-layer ReLU net (64-128-10) on sklearn digits, 1500 images, minibatch 32, WSD sweep with peak rate tuned per point, 5 seeds, measured noise slope 0.56 vs ||grad f||^2

Useful mainly as a warning that 'Muon is normalized therefore decay hard' is not a safe inference.
statement: On a real (non-toy) training task with directly measured gradient noise, Adam's optimal cooldown fraction was 0 and strong cooldown made the final loss worse, because Adam's update stops being Theta(1)-normalized near interpolation.

comparator: full WSD sweeps cf in {0,0.05,...,0.95} on quadratic, (L0,L1) quartic, deep linear net, and digits MLP, versus the 0.2-0.35 cooldown fractions reported to work in LLM pretraining literature

Stated as a limitation by the authors themselves, so internal validity is high but its actionability is low; it should be used to veto schedule proposals that justify themselves purely by noise-structure reasoning.
statement: Stationary landscape-plus-noise models, including the authors' own, appear structurally unable to produce the interior cooldown fractions (~0.2-0.35) that work well in real LLM pretraining; the predicted optima are always 0 or a broad plateau near full decay.

The actionable reading is negative: do NOT propose moving embeddings/lm_head onto Muon; the failure mode is enormous, not marginal.
statement: Applying a stateless / uniformly normalizing update to the embedding matrix instead of an adaptive per-parameter optimizer causes a catastrophic degradation in pretraining perplexity, even with a tuned learning rate.

comparator: original SinkGD with sqrt(nm) Frobenius-norm matching to Adam updates, same LLaMA 270M-1.3B runs

Treat as a hypothesis that the Muon/AdamW update-RMS ratio is a real lever, not as evidence that changing it helps.

comparator: Lion-Hybrid run at the identical learning rates as SAGE, same LLaMA 270M/0.6B/1.3B setup, 3 seeds

Discounted because it is demonstrated on a sign-based (Lion) update, not on AdamW or Muon, and because the higher-lr benefit was never separated from the damper itself -- there is no run of SAGE at Lion's lr and Lion at SAGE's lr other than the collapse. ~40k-step horizon, again far longer than ours.

comparator: AdamW under the same (GC) curvature and (HT) noise assumptions; no experiments are run in this paper

It is registered only because it is the theoretical backdrop for preferring a matrix/sign method on hidden weights (which our config already does) and because it flags that the AdamW side of our hybrid has no guarantee under the noise model that LM pretraining actually exhibits. Not usable by the direction controller and should not be counted as support for any experiment.

comparator: AdamW in the equal-memory regime beta2=beta1, where the target heavy-tailed rate is recoverable in the weighted metric
